utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you continue with Mr. Vulliamy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we begin with Mr. Vulliamy, Mr. Niemann, we have received the motion that you filed yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has the Defence received a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That needs to be discussed in closed session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we will at the appropriate time, after we have concluded Mr. Vulliamy, discuss that in closed session. The motion that you filed regarding -- have a seat, Mr. Vulliamy ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The extension of time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- extension of time, we can also talk about, even though we had given the Defence 14 days to respond to that. The delayed transmission equipment is not fully installed, but I am told that it will be installed fully by Tuesday. I was told that you think that we will continue through today or most of the day with Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We think so, your Honour. We may have some time this afternoon to do those matters though.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had suggested through Miss Featherstone that the Prosecution proceed with the next witness and just be very careful with the witness, but you rejected that suggestion, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not have a witness here, unfortunately, at the moment. We have moved a little faster than we expected. We had tried to put something in place last night, but it was not thought possible to bring the witness forward anyway, but we do not anticipate -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not have the next witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have moved forward at a much faster rate than we expected.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you are responsible for having your witnesses here and available to present them. If they have to wait longer than what is expected, that is unfortunate. I am certainly very concerned for their inconvenience, but our convenience as a Tribunal is more important. So have your witnesses here and available, because we are spending a lot of time. That is absolutely no excuse. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Hopefully, your Honours, it will not be a problem, because this witness -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not "hopefully", there will not be a problem any more. You have your witnesses here and ready to present them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I certainly will. THE PRESIDING JUDGE (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, you understand you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, when we closed yesterday, you had been describing your experiences as you accompanied that convoy of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from Sanski Most. You left off at that point where you were greeted by a soldier from the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina who said that he had buses waiting. Can you describe the impact on the members of that group from Sanski Most when that soldier greeted them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, we were at the end of -- they were at the end of eleven hours of being herded through a gauntlet and three hours walking through a battle and two hours walking over a mountain, and here was this man talking about buses. Some of the older people cried -- I think they felt their journey was over -- with sort of relief and confusion; some were too dazed really to know what was going on. I recall some old women going up and touching the insignia on the side of his arm, as though it was a sort of talisman, just a symbol of their safety, I suppose. Yes, they thought they were safe and they were glad to be alive. It had been quite a day, that had begun for them, as they said, with them being pulled out of their homes that very morning; it was now about some 18 hours or so later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you then describe your impressions as you entered Travnik, the town of Travnik, on those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was now 3.00 in the morning. The places on the buses were allocated for the women and the children and the elderly, others walked, and the large group of 1600 people were split up and organised and taken to -- and this was quite a shock -- any public building, schools, gymnasium or sports halls, whatever, where spaces were found on the floor for them in places that were already teeming with people, other people; and it did not take long to ascertain that all these people had come also from the same Prijedor/Banja Luka region and had come down the same road as us, many, many thousand -- we later established how many. But what was happening at that point was that people were trying to find a space of floor to camp down on and to unpack that which they had been able to manage with them on foot in the dead of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The following day, did you have an opportunity to speak to the people from the convoy about what had occurred to them in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, both that night before we went to -- we ourselves were billeted in a room full of wounded soldiers actually -- and the following day. Both people from our convoy whom we had known and recognised and other people who had been on that same road which, as you can understand, there was quite a sort of bond by this point. They talked about how and why they had been forced to leave. I remember one doctor, in particular, talking about how he felt guilty because his wife and two female friends had been in a front room through which and into which a grenade had been thrown from the street. He had been in the bathroom at the back and survived and been obliged to leave. Others said that men had come to their houses and they had been told they had 24 hours to get out or they would be killed; that sort of story and variations on that theme continued throughout the day and, indeed, throughout the next three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you also have the opportunity to speak to other people in the town who had come from other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were the people from Sanski Most. They were the ones with whom we had travelled. But, yes, they had come from all over the Bosnian Krajina area, Prijedor, Banja Luka area, most notably from the town of Kozarac and from Prijedor itself, from other villages around Banja Luka, a town called Klucj, in particular, that whole area. This was the -- this was unknown to the outside world at that time -- as it were, the dumping ground, this town, Travnik, was the dumping ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did those individuals from these other areas relate similar stories to those that you heard from the people of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if can put it this way, each story was different, but each story was the same; violence, intimidation, deportation and they were almost perversely, because of the sort of place they were now in, quite relieved to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had they all been forcibly transported down that same road, turned over to the local paramilitaries at the border and then forced across, as your group had been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pattern was almost identical, yes. The police had escorted them. We all talked about this place called Smet (which I mentioned yesterday) at which the cars were taken, yes, every time. Then they had walked across this No Man's Land over the same rocks, through the same battle field; the only difference was that some had gone straight along the road if there was no fighting that night, others, if there had been fighting, had gone over the mountain like us. But the story was more or less the same throughout, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At that time did you get any estimate as to how many refugees were in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following day, we were told that there were 36,000 definitely and then others that they maybe had not been able to account for who had not registered. 50,000 was the top figure we heard by then, and this is the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Travnik on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion only until the following day. One had one's professional duties to perform, and our priority was to get to a telephone rather quickly, as you might understand, and that nearest telephone was at Split. So we arranged for transport to take us down to the Croatian coast where we could communicate what we had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was your experience with this convoy from Sanski Most the first reported instance of someone accompanying one of these convoys of forcibly displaced people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was the first and, as far as I know, the only time that people had -- that people from the outside had accompanied such a convoy all the way, as it were, from the inside, rather than greet such convoys as they came through the crossing points which was quite common. But, yes, I think we were the first -- I know we were the first and I think the only to actually accompany such a convoy all the way through the gauntlet, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Subsequent to your experience, did the ICRC issue a document which described similar accounts of treatment of non-Serbs from the Banja Luka area and their forcible transfer over the same route to Travnik as you had experienced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the International Committee of the Red Cross did then verify our findings in a report of their own. There is a document, I think, which says, talks about the difficulties people were having in the Banja Luka region, and talks about them coming over the mountains, along the road into this town of Travnik, about the difficulties in the town in (inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could ask that this document be marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit which will be 182 and then shown to the witness, please? (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the document to which you just referred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 182 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): During this same period of time that we are speaking of, were there statements being made by Serb officials in the Banja Luka region and by the Serb media which reinforced the impression of the people you spoke to that this was a dangerous and organised activity and would continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There were statements being made by the leaders of all the communities and in all their mass media, including those of the, as it were, engineers of this, as it appeared to us, that this was a campaign, that it was organised and it was intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are there any of those particular statements which stand out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a leader article in a Belgrade magazine called Epoka which was photocopied for me by my translator earlier on in Belgrade, which said that if Muslims did not fly white flags or white sheets, or whatever, from the minarets of their mosques, then those villages would be erased. This was translated for me; and, indeed, when working in the Prijedor area during this summer we did see a lot of these white flags, sheets, pillow cases, hanging from minarets, trees sometimes, or windows or washing lines or whatever. The other thing I recall was -- this was a colleague of mine who worked for the same newspaper called Ian Trainer, did some work with an office in Banja Luka that was organising, as they put it, transportations. This was being run, among others, by a man called Vukic who was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, a senior member. He was telling my colleague that he hoped to get rid of 20,000 Muslims in a given period of time and get them to Zenica, which was a Muslim held town, if possible. My colleague talked to other people in that office, published an article about that episode in which people had said that, well, if this was difficult and these -- they were hoping to get some Serbs back from Zenica in exchange -- if this was difficult, they would make life so difficult for the Muslims that they would want to go anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Later on in 1992, in October, was a statement released by the UNHCR from Banja Luka which indicated that, in fact, that was the case, that the Muslims were so desperate to leave that the UNHCR felt compelled to assist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that coming out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document marked next, please? It will be No. 183. (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it -- I remember this statement coming from the UNHCR, from their headquarters, talking about the last stages of ethnic cleansing and "horrible things", and also confirming the systematic nature, in the eyes of this organisation who had people in Banja Luka, that was being carried out with, as they called it, "enormous repression".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender Prosecution 183.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 183 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, could you have that put on the elmo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Or is it a very long article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, it is just the one page. If you could place it on the elmo?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you arrange it so that we can see the top? MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): This is the article to which we were just referring, Prosecution Exhibit 183, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As it indicates, it was issued on 9 October 1992 by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall them releasing it. I think we wrote articles recording its release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that sufficient, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, did you return to Travnik soon after your first trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went back some three-and-a-half weeks later and, in fact, on and off made the town my sort of base camp for the ensuing year, but that return visit was an interesting one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the main impressions or events that you recall from that return visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the first thing was that the numbers of these refugees or deportees, whatever we want to call them, had increased yet more and immeasurably so. People were talking about, I think, 76,000 to 80,000 refugees now in the town. People were now having to sleep out in the open as well in these packed buildings; and the situation was very difficult within those buildings in terms of sanitation and so on. So the place was chocabloc with refugees. They had all come down that same road, all in the manner I have just described, and with one exception which was the second discovery of that return visit. There was talk in the town of a massacre of one of these convoys of people on August 21st 1992. That was four days after we had made that journey. So it was pretty resonant and one was grateful, perhaps, that it had happened that night and not our night. But on that same road and in a place I recalled (and still recall vividly) we were hearing reports that 200 to 250 men had been taken off the buses and out of their cars if they had been driving them to the edge of a ravine and executed. I remember the ravine well, and this was in the early stages -- it was only a few days after that I was back in Travnik -- the early stages of investigating and reporting this. I sought witnesses; there were none in town, but I did later speak to somebody who had been a survivor of that in another town -- this is a long time later -- and I think some video tapes were made. But that was the second discovery, that this massacre had taken, that these attacks on the convoys of which we had seen, as I tried to explain yesterday, remnants literally, human remnants, of such attacks had culminated or grown into a specific massacre of large numbers of people. That was the second thing -- important discovery on the return visit. The third was a conversation I had with a man who described his detention along with about 100 other Muslims in a very small village outside the town of Donji Vakuf which is near Travnik but on Serbian held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: By the time you had that conversation with that man about that camp in Donji Vakuf, you had already experienced first-hand, camps in Bosnia-Herzegovina, had you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you among one of a group of three of the first journalists allowed into the camps at Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I had been one of those three reporters who had gone into Omarska and to Trnopolje camps earlier in the summer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What struck you as so telling about this small camp in Donji Vakuf that was related to you by this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the camps that we had uncovered in the Prijedor region, Omarska and Trnopolje, were fairly large camps, but what this man was talking about was a little shed in which 100 men had been detained. He described how some of them had been murdered, beaten to death, and he described what the Commander of this little camp said to him which was, with a smile, I remember him saying: "The journalists have found the big camps up near Prijedor, but they will never find you down here". This man was later exchanged and got to Travnik, but had no idea what had happened to -- sorry, along with 19 others, but had no idea what had happened to the other 80 whom he had not seen again. I thought, well, that is just a shed, that is just 80 people, but then it dawned on me that, well, that is one shed, what about other sheds that potentially, although we had been able to identify big camps up in the Prijedor region, specifically Omarska and Trnopolje, and others had emerged subsequently, these were, had been, I mean, the keepers of these camps, if that is the right word, had been unable to hide these from us any longer, but goodness knows how many other little places there were. What this man was describing was the potential for sheds, barns, back yards, in any village, in any country village, being used to detain and to, in this case anyway, murder people and beat them. So, one got this impression of a sort of a network of detention that we really were not going to be able to get a grasp of, simply because this place that he had described was so isolated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you continue to witness similar instances of forced displacement, ethnic cleansing, if you will, throughout the conflict right up through 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at first hand all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, in circumstances that differed according to region, but the net result was always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 181 returned to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you just one question while that is being given to you, 181? The article in 183, Mr. Vulliamy, says that there were people who were desperate to leave. If someone were reading that article, could someone reasonably conclude that "desperate to leave" means that they voluntarily wished to leave this area because there has been a change in leadership and they wished to go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose the other language used in that article and, more importantly, what I saw from my own experience was that, as you rightly say, the change in leadership was one that was creating circumstances that made them desperate to leave. I mean, they did not appear to be desperate to leave because they did not approve of the views expressed by that new leadership. I mean, everything that I saw with my own eyes and in all the conversations I had suggested that it was not, you know, like a change of government in my country; that this was a change of leadership which, you know, after which had followed a campaign of violence against these people and that it was that that was making them desperate to leave. It was fear of violence and gunfire and grenades that was making them desperate to leave, not just the fact of a change of leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the person who ran this camp that you referred to as a "shed"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people who, you understand, were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man I spoke to was a Muslim, and he said that the other people in the camp had also been Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 181 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. (To the witness): If you could place the map on the elmo, Mr. Vulliamy, and if you could first simply point out various places in which you witnessed the ethnic cleansing and then we will go back and describe those instances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just, your Honours, a point of clarification the answer to that last question, "Bosnian-Serb" would be the correct answer, not "Serbian". When you say, who ran the shed, it is Bosnian-Serb. I am sorry right. Where are we? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So if you could just point out the various locations beginning in 1992 and up through 1995 where you subsequently witnessed similar instances to those that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my first witness to ethnic cleansing was in an area of a town called Loznica which is right here. Loznica itself is in the east of Serbia close to the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the people in a camp were, a transit place that I went to in Loznica, had come from this area just inside Bosnia-Herzegovina having been threatened and taken there by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the date of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there on August 2nd 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next instance, its location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after that, well, in Travnik after the episodes I have just been describing, there was a dramatic exodus of people, Muslims and Croats, following the fall of a town called Jajce, here in central Bosnia. This town fell and some 50,000 people fled over these mountains here into Turbe and Travnik. That was a massive, a massive movement of people under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From there, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked at various points in 1992 and 1993 in what was then called the Bihac pocket, which is this area here which was held by the Bosnian government, and surrounded -- this area, although it is Croatia, was held by the Croatian Serbs, and this here was held by the Bosnian-Serbs, so it was surrounded completely. Bihac was the main town in that pocket. I spent a great deal of time there, and also at a particularly terrifying place called Bosanska Krupa right here on the river which was the border, if you like, between the government held and the Serbian held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From Bosanska Krupa in the Bihac pocket where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the second half -- sorry, 1993, the spring of 1993, was dominated by the fall or the partial fall of the town of Srebrenica. Here it is. This was not to be confused with the final fall of Srebrenica in 1995. This was, as it were, Srebrenica take one, and people fled from there up to Kladanj here and thence to Tuzla where I was based for a short time, with people flooding into that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second half of 1993, the theme changes somewhat. The most ferocious ethnic cleansing, as we were by then calling it -- forgive the shorthand but that was the word we used -- was not being perpetrated by the Bosnian-Serbs but by the Bosnian-Croats, and it was happening in the area of Herzegovina. This is the Croatian, predominantly Croatian bit of the country down here, and the expulsions were mainly of Muslims from the towns like Capljina, Ljubuski, Citluk, and culminating in the siege of Mostar, the Muslim bit of Mostar there. There were also, by the way, camps but we might like to, sort of, talk about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From there what were the next two significant instances that you observed and witnessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I returned in 1995, we had the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa in the summer of that year. I was there, in particular, for the fall of Zepa, the second of those two, and people were once again coming across here to Kakanji, and thence to Zenica where I was based at the time. There it is there in central Bosnia. There was a sort of final episode in 1995 which took one rather symbolically and depressingly back to square one, spending time here in Travnik and Turbe once again, people were still coming through from the Prijedor region three years later, again down the same road as I had travelled three years before; so it is right through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What I would like to do now is take you back to each of those instances and discuss them; the first being Loznica which you have pointed out on the map. For this examination, we will need the video tape, the first segment of the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is this an exhibit that is in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Not yet, your Honour. It would be Exhibit 184. If we could run the very first segment, please? If you could stop it there, please. Sorry, you need to back up just slightly to that initial building. Thank you. (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the sports hall of a school complex in Loznica which I identified earlier in the eastern part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When approximately were you at that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there on August 2nd 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run to the next segment, please, and stop. I realise that it is a rather difficult shot but, as the tape plays, I think it will become clearer. What was this perspective of? What was the camera looking at here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is happening here is that these are the roofs in front of us of the buildings next to the school which was being used as a transit camp, it was full of people, and what we are looking at is the village from which they had come. It is a hillside, that sort of blue, turquoise bit is a hillside, and that is within Bosnia-Herzegovina because we are so close to the border. We are looking at the village that the people encamped in the school, had been sent away from, from where they had lived, it is called Sepak. It was so close that they could see it from the place in which they were encamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of those people who came from that village which you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who were the people who were running the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the police of the Republic of Serbia proper rather than Bosnian-Serbs dressed in blue uniforms. This place was in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could continue running the video and with the audio. Your Honours, it appears that the best audio actually comes by wearing the headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could stop the video there, please? This gentleman, Mr. Vulliamy, is this one of the individuals who were interviewed by the group of reporters that went to Loznica that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I should say that this material was shot by the ITN crew with whom I was in Belgrade. They had gone down there the previous day, on August 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The woman talking to this man, that would be Penny Marshal, one of the reporters who was with you on that trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my colleague, Penny Marshal of ITN, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The man mentioned the village of Subotica. They were supposed to be taken to the village of Subotica. Where is Subotica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Subotica is right up in the north of Serbia close to the Hungarian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that story repeated to you with the individuals whom you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely, they were all told the same thing. They were told that they were going to go -- they said they had been told they were going to go to Subotica and thence to Germany or Austria. That was just the same, if I may say so, as the people from Sanski Most had been told on the convoy that I was on, that, you know, "the papers are in order, you are going to Germany or Austria". That is what everybody I spoke to here as well had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The following description which this man gives of what occurred and his impression of it, is it consistent with the interviews, all of interviews, which were conducted in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, yes absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could play the rest of that tape with the audio?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 184?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I was going to tender it at the end at the end ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: After we have seen it all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- of this segment, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could stop it there? I would tender that segment of the tape, your Honour, at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 184 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, did you yourself go over to the village of Zepa in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I interviewed an older man who could also see his house from the camp. He tried to point it out to me. In fact, he issued the same sort of challenge as that young man. He said: "You can go to my house, I cannot". So I said: "Well, OK, I will".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, go over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How did you get over to the village of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very easily. My translator and guide said that we take the car down to a small bridge, there is a crossing over the river which was also the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said it would be less trouble to park the car and walk across, and we did. Nobody asked to see anything; we just walked across.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you crossed the border, were you required to show any sort of identification at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all, no, just walked across it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was anyone being stopped and asked for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I could see, no. Most of the traffic in both directions was military and they were not being asked to show any ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you say "military", can you describe type of uniforms that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were in the uniforms of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How could you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew it well from the war in Croatia, from -- well, indeed, from day, previous day. I mean, it was a familiar uniform to me by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What insignia did they have on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were still wearing the old red star from the communist era, one or two, on the front of their helmets, if they had helmets, or on other parts of their uniform. Some had no insignia and some had the emerging insignia of the new Serbia, if you like, the post Yugoslav Serbia, which was an eagle, a two headed eagle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What type of activity was going on along and across that border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the majority of the traffic in both directions was military, although there were some civilians going to and from as well. Loznica was a largely militarized town at that point. I described yesterday the atmosphere in the towns of Sid and Bogojevo in Eastern Serbia near the Croatian border, and here we had something fairly similar in Loznica. There were a lot of trucks, soldiers hanging around the cafes, yards with military vehicles parked and just military traffic coming and going, some soldiers on foot, others in private cars, others in mini buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see transport of military equipment and men going across the border from the Republic of Serbia into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on that occasion I did not see any heavy tanks or anything but, yes, there were small amoured vehicles were travelling to and fro, yes, and mostly from the Serbian side into the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of the soldiers about what they were doing in that area, what the purposes of this movement of military personnel and equipment were for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very anecdotally. I did not want to draw attention to myself. I did not feel particularly safe, despite the ease with which we had crossed border. So it was fairly sort of jovial, you know: "How long have you been here?" They would say: "Oh, a few days". "Everything OK?" "Yes, it is quiet here now"; that sort of banter. I did not have any in-depth conversations with them. I did not particularly want to draw attention to myself on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was it clear to you who was in control of that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very clear indeed, the Yugoslav People's Army, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did all of these soldiers, regardless of the insignia which they wore at the time, appear to you to act as one unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, there was no reason to believe that they were not. They were - some of them were, sort of, casually patrolling, others were attaching flags to the lampposts in the village of Sepak which we eventually reached, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the areas where the equipment was stored and the men were billeted, were individuals with all of the various types of insignia working together without distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, the men, as far as I could gather, were billeted and the operation was, sort of, based in Loznica on the Serbian side, I mean, all the -- I was not there long, but it was long enough to realise that all the, as it were, vehicle maintenance, that sort of thing -- I am sorry to be so vernacular about it, but, you know, the drink in the evening, that was all happening in Loznica over on the Serbian side. Sepak was just a tiny village, so I do not think there were many soldiers staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who was guarding the actual camp in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were they wearing the regular police uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who did the people that you interviewed in the camp tell you had brought them to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers from -- actually, they were not particularly clear where they were from. I mean, they just talked about "the army", "the soldiers" had arrived. Once I got into the village, we could see there had been some fire straight across some of the houses, but they just talked about "soldiers", "the army", "the military".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You did, in fact, make it to the village of Sepak yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find that old man's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am pretty sure I did, yes. His description matched roughly what I found, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there anyone living in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Bosnian-Serb family from the Sarajevo suburbs, a suburb called Gobavica, who said that their house had been on the front line there and had been destroyed and they had been relocated to Sepak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did they have any comments for the former owner of the house which they asked you to relate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not seem that concerned. When I talked to the former owner of the house, he had asked a fellow -- if I could just in parenthesis here for the sake of clarity -- in the Loznica camp, or the transit camp, there was a part for Muslims and another part for Serbs. The Serbs had beds, I would hasten to add, and the Muslims did not. There were Serbian refugees around as well at that time. They were putting some of them up in this place too. Anyway, this gentleman had asked one of the Serbs, as it were, on the other side of the camp to telephone his house to see if there was anybody there. He had done so, there was and, if you will forgive an anecdote, the message to him was, could he please call back some time and tell him how the washing machine worked. So I knew that there was somebody there already. It was a Serbian family from Sarajevo. They did not seem to care much about the people who had left, although they, sort of, said: "Well, it is a pity, it is a shame", but they said: "It is not a crime or it is not theft of any kind because our house was blown up by Muslim guns in Sarajevo, so we have a Muslim house in return". They were fairly unperturbed and they liked the DIY that he had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After you left Loznica, was that the trip from where you then went on to Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same, as it were, chapter. We were at Omarska within a couple of days of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The next aspect of the ethnic cleansing, as you referred to it, that you experienced, you said, was Jajce in the fall of 1992. Could you describe what you witnessed in Jajce and when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the period between September and October 1992. Jajce was a small town and a tourist attraction just to the north west of Travnik. It was held by the Muslim Croat alliance, as it then was, and attached to Travnik by a sort of umbilical cord, a corridor, through which you could get up to Jajce. I tried several times to do that, but each time was beaten back by gunfire across this corridor which was only about 500 metres wide, so I never actually got up to Jajce but got pretty close, and that corridor was littered with vehicles that had been shot off the road, some ambulances and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the map exactly where you get to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is Jajce. At present on this map which is current under Muslim Croat Federation authority, but then the line was sort of here like that at the time, but there was, as I say, this fairly remarkable sort of cord attaching Jajce which was out on a promontory, as it were, from the Federation territory down here. So you would work your way up this corridor at night, of course, only, and this is where all the shooting and the wrecked vehicles were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So you were somewhere in that corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we would go up there, we would stay the night, maybe come back before daylight, and the town eventually fell under what was reported to be particularly ferocious bombardment and the people who were defending it unable to do so any longer. The evacuation was ordered, and we met that evacuation fairly -- about midway between Travnik and Jajce. They started at a place called Karaula halfway up the corridor and it was a remarkable sight. There were in all some (we later counted) 50,000 people making their way along the tracks, and they had with them their animals sometimes, herds of sheep; there were a large number of horse drawn carts, cattle, again old people, children, everybody. They were under fire as they moved towards the relative safety of Travnik. I can remember in the afternoon heat suddenly from -- I mean, we were in, I suppose, theoretically safe territory towards, you know, the place where these people were heading, and a shot rang out from nowhere, and the next thing you knew there was somebody on a cart who had been shot in the arm, a fairly old man; and there were people being transported in wheel barrows and so on. By this time there must have been 90,000 or more people in Travnik and in the surrounding villages which were now being used to billet refugees, add another 50,000 and that was quite a sight. That late afternoon, that night, I can remember every piece of ground in the town, people were encamped with animals, broilers, defeated army. I wrote at the time -- forgive me, sort of, using such language, it looked look like something out of Tolstoi, frankly, this scene of smoke and animals and complete and utter chaos. Later that night it began to rain very hard and we, some of us, joined in trying to find people somewhere to go. The UNHCR had a couple of people down there -- very few. The Red Cross, I think, were coming on, and people were trying to find places to shelter. Then the shells started coming in from what was now a new front line because, the corridor having fallen, the guns had moved up just that day or, at least, mortars had been moved up. I can remember the day ending with this almost, sort of, adding insult to injury, they started shelling the places where the refugees were encamped on the streets of this town. Some were injured. I can remember people were just running from this shell fire which lasted for about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did the people that were coming out of Jajce describe what had happened in those final days in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had described living mostly underground during the last days. They said that when food supplies had reached them up the corridor, they had gone out to queue for them and the queues for the food had been attacked. They said that there was no way they could stay there any longer. The soldiers were saying that the defence of the town was unsustainable. Most memorably, people were just talking about watching their house hit, or one man said he saw his house on fire as he left. People were talking about scrambling up muddy banks. They were talking about the retreat from the town under fire. One man talked about seeing somebody shot in the head right in front of him as he had retreated. There it was a comfortless, a comfortless story.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Subsequent to your trip in October, did the ICRC issue a release about this very operation the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember they arrived in Travnik and I can remember their account of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If could I have this document marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit No. 185 and then shown to the witness, please? (Exhibit 185 was handed to the witness) (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the press release they put out , in fact, during the fall of the town. It was after the first couple of days with more people still on the road for whom we were waiting on these newly established front lines, much closer to the town of Travnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could place that on the elmo, please, for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 185?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That first paragraph that is describing the numbers of persons coming from Jajce and the fact that the sheltering capacity of Travnik at that point was exhausted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, exactly. They had obviously better access to the exact numbers than we did at the time, but all I can say is that both out on the roads, or mountain tracks as I should properly call them, and coming into the town, I mean, they were vast, vast numbers of people. I mean, our convoy of 1600 had seemed vast enough; here was what I think was one of the biggest exoduses of the war. I see the ICRC are putting the total at something like 50,000 in all or 30,000 in Travnik at the time they wrote this document with another 20,000 expected to be -- expected to come in and still out on the road. That was about the estimated population of the town at the time, made up of residents and also from refugees from surrounding areas, including the Prijedor region who had fled into that town, into Jajce, as well as into Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this same time, in October and November 92, were there, in addition to your experiences in the Jajce area, continuing notifications from the ICRC and the High Representative for the Human Rights Commission about the continued ethnic cleansing and mistreatment of non-Serbs in the Banja Luka/Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were frequent and, in particular, from the latter source you have mentioned, the United Nations High Commission for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have these next two documents marked, please? They will be exhibits 186 and 187. (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, if you could review those one at a time and then place them on the elmo, please? Do you recognise No. 186?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a man called Beat Schweizer. He is the head of the Red Cross, the International Committee of the Red Cross office that had been established in Banja Luka since late June, and he is giving an interview here to the Austrian radio which I believe is -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could place that on the elmo, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In this particular article he is describing the conditions that he is aware of in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he starts off talking about the camp which, as we knew by then, was a place into which people from the Banja Luka region had been collected, and he is saying that it is getting out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would offer Exhibit 186.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 186 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Now the next Exhibit 187. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is an agency report of the Agence France Press reporting one of the many reports compiled by Tadeuz Mazowiecki who was the United Nations High Representative from the Commission on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If you could place that on the elmo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was one of his many articles about and denunciations of, in this case, ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This was issued after his visit to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In which he described the circumstances as he saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would offer Exhibit 187.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 187 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could move that to the bottom, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does 187 explain why the 100 to 200,000 or so persons referred to in 186 wanted to leave the area, Mr. Vulliamy? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. 187 is about the Trnopolje camp which we found during the summer of 1992. The significance of it, as it were, at this stage of the discussion is that it was to Trnopolje that many people were brought from their homes and villages or, indeed, fled from their homes and villages because their homes and villages were burning down or under shell fire, and from there that by this time people were being sent on those convoys that we are talking about. So Trnopolje is, as it were, the staging post, was by this time the staging post, the transit camp, the place from which people from all sorts of different circumstances in the Prijedor region (which, perhaps, we will move on to later) were coming to for a variety of reasons and, thereafter, were being either herded over the mountains (as we were) into Travnik or being taken there by, as happened later, the Red Cross. Trnopolje was, if you like, the distribution point for this process, or one of them -- one of the many, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Keegan. I do not mean to interrupt. I guess again my focus is really a concern about what happens in times of war and people may want to leave for a number of reasons. I wanted to find out how 187 and 186 were connected and whether or not this was a forced expulsion or a desire once again on the part of people to leave, but I think the witness has explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and I think also if the court considers this exhibit in line with all the other testimony from the other witnesses who have come previously describing what events were occurring in that region throughout this time. (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, if we could now move on to the next situation which you had indicated you witnessed which was the Bihac pocket area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Bihac was important for a number of reasons. It was described by the United Nations because it was this pocket, there was a tranche of Serbian held territory, Prijedor, Banja Luka, this area, very loosely connected to Serbia through a corridor. Then there was, if I may say so, the Croatian Serbian bit, the Krajina in Croatia where Serbs were living. So the Bihac pocket was, as the United Nations soldiers put it, a bone in the throat of that tranche of land which the Serbs wanted, had actually, but they wanted, this was the pocket in its throat, as the soldiers put it. It was subject to particularly ferocious attack at various stages of the war and, also importantly, it was yet another dumping ground because it was adjacent to the Prijedor region. It was another place, yet another place, as we realised when we went there, for deportees, refugees, people fleeing, people in flight, people forced into flight, however we are going to put it. There are two places I would like to talk about, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, you first mentioned Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosanski Krupa was one of the most frightening places I have been to in the whole war. It was right on the River Una which was the border between the edge of the Muslim held Bihac pocket and the Bosnian Serb territory, and so the two sides, if that is the word, were separated only by the width of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you get into that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A long, long walk. We drove to a place call Cazim nearby and then walked down a hillside, or in some places ran down the hillside because the snipers could see us and were shooting at us, into the town which was on the valley floor next to the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you find once you were in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a shooting gallery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The United Nations had not been there. The Red Cross had not been there at that time. This is September 1992, the first time I went there. No supplies had got in there and people were living off the fruit that they had grown on their trees and the food that they had grown in their gardens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did they harvest that fruit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They used to just dig it up and the place was -- I hasten to add, also there were large numbers of refugees from the Prijedor area living there as well, having fled across the river from the Serbian territory. What people would have to do -- I will have to explain this, sort of, with gestures as well as words, if I may -- is that to go out anywhere in the town, the houses were right along the river, you would have to hide behind a house, run to the next house and, as you did so, "clack, clack", the snipers would shoot at you. (Indicating) You would run and you would stop, and then you would run again to the next house. That was how people moved around the town. That is how we moved around the town. We asked how many people had been killed during this. We were told 56 during the two weeks preceding our visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How many forces from the Bosnian Army were resident in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but very few. I mean, there was a thing called a police station which was basically a house and there were about, sort of, I suppose, 20 to 50 soldiers mooching about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very few -- rifles, a few machine guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of all of the people that you met in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslim with one Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had you also on some occasion had the opportunity to discover what forces were aligned on the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the Bosnian-Serb Army and it was pretty clear what weaponry they had from what was starting to come into Bosanska Krupa as night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mortars and shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the conditions that the people were living under in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Terrifying. They were living in their cellars, if they had any. One man had a cellar in which he put a lot of people, in which he offered to fit people, neighbours, when the shelling got particularly heavy; otherwise they were just sitting in their houses. Some of the houses were destroyed, obviously, and people were sort of living in, as it were, the fire shadows, as we would call it, of the walls that remained of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you spend in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During that time was this sniper fire, as you explained it, constant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was sniper fire during the day with the odd mortar coming in and then the heavier stuff would come in towards evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you get out of that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We played the cat and mouse game. We ran between the houses and, yes, bullets, you know, you could hear them whizzing past us. Then we had to run up the track back out of the town which is what the fitter citizens of the place had done, by definition, leaving behind the more elderly people who represented a disproportionate numbers of the population because they obviously could not run up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that the only way into or out of that village at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the only viable way. There was a road down to Bihac which the UN eventually navigated sometime later, but to drive down that road was suicidal at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As compared to running up the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You were a lot safer running up the hill than you were driving, let alone walking, down the road because the road skirted the river and you were just, I mean, you were fully exposed; you would not have had a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From Bosanksa Krupa did you move into the town of Bihac itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation that met you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bihac, like Travnik, was full of refugees mostly from the Prijedor/Banja Luka region. I remember, in particular, one group of people who were living in a network of tunnels and underground cellars that the German army had dug, built, in the Second World War. The shelling was sometimes very heavy indeed, and we took refuge in one of these tunnels one afternoon. I remember, as one became accustomed to the darkness, a fairly extraordinary sight, just these people eating soup or lying on makeshift beds in these tunnels, mostly old people, some from Bihac itself, the majority from Prijedor and the surrounding villages who had fled into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of conditions were they living under in those tunnels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very difficult conditions, both physically and psychologically. It was dark all the time. They were getting food. They would send people out to get food from the aid organisations. They were mumbling. They were people who were too terrified. They were old people for the most part who were just too afraid to go out. One old lady I interviewed at length, she was 80 something, she remembered the Second World War. She said: "It was nothing like this", and one had this awful feeling that she was going to end her days down there. They were -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there sufficient lighting down in these tunnels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the lighting was coming through grates at the upper part of the tunnels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there adequate bedding for everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was somewhere to lie down. They had constructed, sort of, very primitive bunks for some of the older people. A few were sleeping on the floors. No, there was not adequate bedding. They had done their best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there running water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there kitchens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had, sort of, camper stoves that they were making soup on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did any of the people from the Prijedor/Banja Luka region whom you spoke to indicate that they had voluntarily left their homes to come to these conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was one young woman we spoke to, typically -- and forgive the detail -- when she realised she was going to be interviewed by foreigners, she sort of disappeared for about 10 minutes and came back made up, which I thought was rather sort of tragic in its way. She told a terrifying story about having been burnt out of her house in a village near Prijedor. She described their marching, they were marched down the road, she said, by soldiers. She said that sometimes they would open fire, but usually they were just going, "Get on, get on, get on". She described how she and a friend of hers had peeled off from that convoy towards night and had come through the woods into Bosanska Krupa, in fact. The Serbs there -- she said the Serbs had kept them a few days to make coffee, but then they had allowed them to cross the river into Bosanska Krupa. She had come from there to Bihac. That was one of the many stories we heard. She was now living in this tunnel. I said: "Why are you living in this tunnel? You are a young woman, you could be living in the town". She said: "I am too afraid of the explosions to go out. I never go out".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were in Bihac did you, in fact, witness yourself an attack from the forces on the other side of the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several attacks, and we were shot at actually driving down a road from the Croatian Serbian side of the pocket; fire coming from, as it were, not the Bosnian Serb side but the Croatian Serb side, and this was confirmed by the UN as a fairly regular thing, shelling and shooting. There was one attack I particularly remember on the Bihac hospital where I spent quite a bit of time. A shell came into the hospital and a man recovering from another attack was wounded in this hospital bed. Something even more memorable happened in that hospital actually. A seven year old girl died more less in my arms, well, not in my arms, but my hand on her. She had been shot in the head by a sniper while, I was told, running across her back garden with her mother running from an explosion, and a sniper had caught her in the head which was all bandaged up and you could not, sort of, see her face very well. She was unconscious and the doctor said: "Come and see this girl?" and I had a photographer with me who took a photograph. I just had my hand on her shoulder, and as I did so there was a kind of quiver and a shake, and the panic, doctors all over the place. I stood back. They came in and that was, in fact, her death at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that the attack which you had yourself witnessed had come from the area of the Republic of Serb Krajina. If you could indicate on the map the area which you were referring to, please, to Exhibit 181?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is the Bihac pocket. Here is what we call the Bosnian Krajina -- sorry, if I am confusing -- this is the Prijedor/Banja Luka region held by the Bosnian Serbs. Here is the bit marked on the map as Croatia which is called the Croatian Krajina held at that time by the Croatian Serbian forces and, although most of the attacks would logically come here from the Bosnian Serb side, this shooting was from the Croatian side, Serbs here on the Croatian side into the pocket. Bihac is there, and there are actually roads and communities skirting this border. This area was under the tutelage of the United Nations soldiers policing the peace in Croatia at the time. It was with some disdain, I might add, that the UN military observers within Bihac itself confirmed that the attacks from this side, from this UN protected zone within Serbian held Croatia, were fairly regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document marked as the next exhibit please, 188? (To the witness): While that document is being marked, Mr. Vulliamy, was there any doubt or hesitation in the military command or in the UN officials that you talked to in Bihac that the attacks were being conducted in a co-ordinated fashion between the Bosnian Serbs and the Croatian Serbs against Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely no doubt at all. There was the United Nations military observer team there, was headed by a Norwegian, the deputy was British and neither of them -- in fact, they were one of the angriest military, team of military observers I had come across in the whole war for that very reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they describe to you that the attacks were conducted by large scale groups of the army of the Bosnian Serbs and the Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, indeed, and they were also confirming bombing from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were many of those reports from the Bihac pocket later down played by senior UNPROFOR and UN officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the Bihac pocket went through various crises during its history, and particularly the reports from the ground that we had confirmed over and over again that an underground aerodrome, an airfield, within the Serbian held bit of Croatia was being used by fighter bombers which were bombing the Bihac pocket. We were taken up to see the results of such bombing and, yes, pretty clear from the craters that this was bombing from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could place Exhibit 188 on the elmo, please, for the court? Do you recognise that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise the facts in it, but that is a report from Belgrade that I do not -- I mean, I do not know that particular account of the facts but I recognise the facts well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is this the report, one of the reports, you mentioned that initially indicates that troops from the Republic of Serb Krajina, that is, the Croatian Serb territory was attacking the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is UNPROFOR, United Nations Protection Force, confirming in April 1993 what we had already been told in August, sorry, September, forgive me, 1992, that these attacks were coming not only from the Bosnian Serb side but from within what they called the RSK, the Serbian Krajina part of Croatia, as well, so that this place is surrounded and being attacked from all sides, one in coordination with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does that report also indicate that by the time the report from the field which indicated a force of 1,000 troops had reached Zagreb, it was then revised by the headquarters in Zagreb to be 100 to 150?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. From Bihac, Mr. Vulliamy, you indicated that you then next witnessed a similar activity in the Tuzla Srebrenica situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Tuzla briefly during the spring of 1993. The town of Srebrenica was unreachable at the time, and the collapse and surrender of the town was being monitored by radio hams with whom we were in contact who were able to talk to Srebrenica on short wave radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, I neglected to offer Exhibit 188.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 188?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): After you received these reports, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all we could do really was to wait for more news and wait for people to come, if they ever were going to come. This was not the fall of Srebrenica that we have heard so much in 1995; this was the point at which the Bosnian-Serb army marched into and shelled the town to such a degree that it surrendered. This was the series of instances that gave way to the safe -- declaration of safe areas of which Srebrenica was one. Basically, we were in Tuzla and the first people started coming in from Srebrenica. I was not able to stay there very long at that time. All I can describe is the trucks of people coming in at the end of a very long journey into Tuzla, another town, I hasten to add, jam packed with refugees from all over the place. They were coming in in a wearisome and distressed state. The Serbian army had not got into the town, but they talked about relentless shelling. I remember one woman saying, in particular, that the streets were so full that you could not but get a direct hit if you put any shell into the streets of that town. I had then to leave Tuzla for other reasons. Subsequent accounts talked about people clambering on to trucks and other people being caught in minefields, but I was not directly taking those testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the same time that you were hearing these reports over the short wave and through the people you were talking to, was again the High Representative for the Human Rights Commission and the UNHCR issuing statements both with regards to the situation in Tuzla and in Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the, as it were, first fall of Srebrenica was one of the major crises in the war internationally. Of course, both Mr. Mazowiecki and the UNHCR were watching it, they were engaged, they were involved and were speaking publicly about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have these next two documents marked as Exhibits 189 and 190, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy -- I am trying to follow your lead, Mr. Keegan -- did you give us a number, an estimate at least, that you could make as to the number of refugees you saw in Bosanska Krupa and Bihac or does Exhibit 188 give us a number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, 188 is -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: 188 has been removed. If you could go ahead and give your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, numbers games, I do not particularly like; I prefer to quote people who make a job of counting numbers, the International Red Cross, the UNHCR and so on. This pertains to numbers of refugees, numbers of dead, numbers of wounded, numbers of people homeless and so on, numbers of missing. It is always difficult for us because one is seeing groups of 20 here, five here, 100 there, and you see a camp full of inestimable hundreds. So it is difficult to say, but in Bosanska Krupa, I would say that a fairly small number, let us say, hundreds not thousands. I would not want to put it any more specific than that. In Bihac, the numbers I saw, well, I saw hundreds in places that suggested there would be thousands, if not tens of thousands, but I would not want to say for a minute to you that I had seen crowds of tens of thousands of people in Bihac. No, I did not. They were too dispersed. People were billeted in all kinds of places, and I am more than happy to try to make estimates for you, but it is not a game I like playing, frankly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you want to discuss Exhibits 189 and 190 quickly or should we stand in recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I think we will be able to wrap it up

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Do you have Exhibits 188?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sorry, 189 and 190?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could review 189 first? Do you recognise what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do indeed. Well, it is an Agence France Press report of a document I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is the report by the Special Raporteur that we referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mazowiecki of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In which he describes the situation in Tuzla. If you can move the document up to the paragraph referring to Tuzla? Just at the bottom of the screen there. That particular section of the report relates to the number of refugees that had actually been registered at that time in Tuzla by the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was it your experience in all of these areas which you visited that the number of registered refugees was not necessarily an accurate reflection of how many were in an area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number of registered refugees was, by definition, the minimum. Those were the people that the International Commission for the Red Cross, or in this case or more usually, the UNHCR, knew were there and who had registered with them. So if one wants to make estimates of numbers, you take that as the base and then one has to depend on one's own assessment to make calculations above that. But, yes, this is Mr. Mazowiecki's estimate of the numbers who were arriving in Tuzla at that time. This is -- the Special Raporteur is by now well into his series of reports.
