This is one of a great number which we were following very closely. I remember this one well. This is the one which, if you will pardon the expression, we referred to as him finally "doing his nut" because he says that "if you do not stop this" -- he addresses the International Community and says, "If you do not stop this, then you are complying with it". We reported those remarks very -- with some shock coming from a man like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would tender Exhibit 189, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 189 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): If you could now take a look at 190, please? Do you recognise that report from the UNHCR representative regarding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is again Agence France Press recording remarks that I remember very well indeed from Larry Hollingsworth who was an ex, former British army soldier now working for the UNHCR who I knew personally, and here he is giving his view of the incident in Srebrenica, the results of which I was seeing in terms of refugees coming into Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If you could move that up, please? Were the shellings and effects of that shelling that was reported in this UNHCR release consistent with those reports that you also received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and consistent with what everybody else was saying. One television journalist called Tony Burkley -- I think only one -- got into Srebrenica at that time, and certainly Mr. Hollingsworth's assessment was borne out by everybody else that I spoke to, whether they were colleagues, refugees, from that. It was one of the low points, as I recall, of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 190.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 190 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I think that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Vulliamy, when we recessed you had just finished describing the situation surrounding the fall of Srebrenica and some of the reports that were coming out at that time about what was happening in East Bosnia. At the same time that this exodus from Srebrenica was occurring and the attack on Srebrenica was being conducted, were government officials from the Bosnian Serb Republic also issuing press statements that both had once responded to allegations about war crimes and also indicated their intent in the conduct of these operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had by now ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turn your microphone on, Mr. Vulliamy, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point I had no direct communication with the Bosnian Serb leadership because I was more or less based on the other side, but I do recall them continuing to make their intention fairly clear to keep up this, as they regarded it, war until its completion to their satisfaction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document please marked as the next exhibit in order, that would be 191, and shown to the witness, please. If you could please review Exhibit 191. That report of a statement by General Milovanovic of the main staff of the Army of the Republika Srspka, is that familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I remember reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In fact the first paragraph, does that refer to one of the statements that you made mention of that referred to their intention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was quite widely reported. When he says that the Serbs in Bosnia would never accept the Drina River as their border, by the "Drina River" he means the -- the Drina River is the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, and what he is saying here is that the Bosnian Serbs would never accept that river as a border, in other words, we are part of that country. It was, as the thing says, a speech he made on the first anniversary of the one of the armies brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would offer Exhibit 191.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 191 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this document marked it will be 192.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a reference to a referendum in here that is not explained. That referendum was a rejection by some 99 per cent of the Vance Owen peace-plan which had been accepted by the other two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you review Exhibit 192, please. What is Exhibit 192?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 192 is an interview by Dr. Karadzic, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. It is an interview he gives to a Turkish radio station or newspaper which I have to admit I did not see or listen to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could place that on the elmo, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. He is discussing the semantics of the term "ethnic cleansing".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does he also make reference to the allegations about the camps as well, down in the middle paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is denying that they are concentration camps; he calls them camps for prisoners of war. This is in response, I expect, to our discoveries of Omarska and Trnopolje in which a number of emaciated prisoners were found and he is talking about a slim boy sent to the camp by accident. He calls all the others very handsome and well-built people. Perhaps in due course we can come to that. But that is Mr. Karadzic's point of view anyway for the record. I do not remember this particular interview because it was to a Turkish media, but I remember him saying similar things to the British and the American media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would offer Exhibit 192, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 192 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Finally, if I could have this document marked as Exhibit 193. During this same time that you were now witnessing the scenes in Eastern Bosnia, did there continue to be reports issued by UNHCR and others about continued ethnic cleansing and forced expulsions in the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the way through, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could review Exhibit 193, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the spring of 1993 and by now we can see the UNHCR engaged in evacuating people along the same route that we would have taken under armed Serbian, Bosnian Serb guard. They are talking about people coming out of the Banja Luka area into central Bosnia. That is the road we took. By "central Bosnia" they mean Travnik at least as the port of entry. So we can now see the UNHCR according to this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The conditions under which the UNHCR report indicate those people had been living, are they similar circumstances to which the people whom you interviewed described to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to me that the gist has not changed. On our convoy and in all the people I interviewed coming in from all sorts of places, markedly the Banja Luka Prijedor region, they were talking about attacks on their homes, terror, murder and so on, and here UNHCR is ratifying this, talking about seven murders in one district.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Again the people being forcibly transferred or deported were expected to pay for that transportation by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Here again the UNHCR is confirming something we had heard over and over again, that this deportation was regarded as something for which a fare was payable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you your Honour I would offer Exhibit 193.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 193 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could also have this next document marked, please. That would be Exhibit 194. Mr. Vulliamy, as we move into 1994 did the reports from these non-governmental organisations, international organisations, in particular the ICRC, become more specific and aggressive in their tone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they became, let us say, more out spoken. The ICRC is well known for its judicious conduct, judicious in the extreme. Its job is to fulfil its professional brief. We had this discussion with its officers over and over again. Its job is not to apportion blame or usually to make didactic remarks, but such is the situation by the time of this press release, which I recall reading about, they are starting to use a more didactic language, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could put the first page of 194 on the screen, please. The first page of this press release gives a summary, a brief summary, of the ICRC's attempts and their opinion on the situation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Summed up by that single sentence in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the state of affairs is unacceptable to the ICRC, they say, and they are talking about civilians being used, as they say, bargaining chips in the interests of political causes, I do not wish to interpret the document, but politics was military by this time in the country as I think is abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you put the second page on. On the second page do they specifically mention the Banja Luka region and then those areas in central Bosnia to which you have referred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, we are our September 1994, this is two years after our convoy out of the Prijedor area, and they are saying that the minorities are being subjected to harassment and discrimination every day; having lost all hope for the future they have no choice but to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When they speak of majorities in the Banja Luka region, what ethnic background are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In central Bosnia and Zenica and in Bihac, in all of those areas, who were the people whom you interviewed which related those tales of forced ethnic cleansing and other crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In central Bosnia leaving the Zenica region, this would be Croats and some Serbs leaving what was by now a very hard line Muslim town. In the Bihac area they would be talking about Muslims and some Croats fleeing from Serbian authority, as I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The figure they use is tens of thousands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In Gorazde, in Srebrenica what populations are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Gorazde, in Srebrenica, well, these are both isolated pockets of overwhelmingly almost exclusively Muslim populations encircled by Serbian guns, so this would be Muslims in those two pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In that following one line paragraph, "In most of these situations it is the Muslim civilian population that is the principal victim of such an abominable policy", do you find that to be a significant statement to be made by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was abundantly clear to anybody who was covering the war that that was the case. It was uncharacteristic of the ICRC to make such a partial remark, if you like, but they appear from the fact they did so, to have regarded the situation as sufficiently serious to have crossed a line that they, from the conversations I had with them personally and from the press releases they put out normally, declined to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would offer Exhibit 195.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, 194.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is the same number we were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For the official record though it is 194 and that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if we could return now to the instances of ethnic cleansing which you referred to earlier that you witnessed. After Tuzla, Srebrenica you indicated in your summary that the next area of ethnic cleansing which you witnessed was in the Mostar Prozor region that had been conducted by Bosnian Croats against Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking here about Prozor in central Bosnia which pertains to late 1992, but throughout the latter half of 1993 the emphasis and shift of the conflict changes. I will just summarise. We were now engaged or I was now engaged mostly in covering the mass deportation of Muslims from the Herzegovina and Lasva Valley areas by Croatian forces. The pattern here was that men were being taken to camps and I was busy gaining access to those camps and did so. The worst was a place called Dretelj where Muslims were being held by Croats, and women and children were by and large being herded by military soldiers into a very small Muslim pocket in the city of Mostar to which a particularly ferocious siege was laid. There were also instances of ethnic cleansing between Muslims and Croats in both directions in central Bosnia, and that took up most of my work for the latter part of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then as we move on to the last couple of instances which you mentioned, one being Zepa in Eastern Bosnia in 1995, if you could describe the circumstances which you found there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fall of the two eastern enclaves held thus far by the Bosnian government in Srebrenica and Zepa, they were both UN safe areas, in 1995 is, I think, fairly well known. My experience was mainly of the latter. I was in the Muslim held town of Zenica when large numbers of people from the fallen enclave, by then fallen enclave of Zepa in eastern Bosnia, were coming into the town. I apologise if this is becoming monotonous, but their accounts were of heavy shelling in a town by now jam packed full of refugees from all over Eastern Bosnia and also from the fallen Srebrenica itself. The town had succumbed to the Bosnian-Serb Army just weeks before. Large numbers of people had fled from one pocket into the other. The pocket had been shelled and people were talking once again about shells landing in crowded streets in which people were sleeping and unable to avoid direct hit on civilians, if you like. There was a negotiated surrender in which the UN acted as broker and the people were evacuated in a fashion which was fairly orderly compared to what we know about Srebrenica without the thousands reported massacred, but it was nevertheless a pretty distressing sight. They came in, some in primitive vehicles, trucks, and some on foot into Zenica. They had been met further up towards the front lines by their own army, the Bosnian Government Army, and brought to Zepa in a fairly orderly way and kept in compounds and fed. We were allowed to go and talk to them and they had talked about the town holding out for as long as it could, but unable to hold out any longer and given what they had heard from the people who had arrived there from Srebrenica, very afraid indeed that the same thing might happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In addition to talking to the people in Zenica who had come out of Zepa, did you talk to Zepa refugees in other locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Ireland, in Dublin of all places. I had a call to tell me that some people had arrived in Dublin from two camps within Serbia itself. This was in the Christmas period of 1995. I was very interested to talk to them because I wanted to know about the camps they had been kept in and also to hear more about what had happened to Zepa. There were 24 of them in all, men, a part of a group which had refused to surrender and had gone off into the wilderness, into the mountains, and then had elected to cross the border into Serbia and to try their luck by surrendering eventually there, not to the Bosnian Serbs of whom they were afraid because they thought they would be massacred, as had happened to their colleagues in Srebrenica. They were put in these camps and told the stories about their travels through to Serbia and about what they had witnessed, people being rounded up on the way and killed and the camps had been hard at first but had improved after the UNHCR and ICRC were made aware of them, and there they were held up in a mental hospital in Dublin, mental hospital because that was the only place they could find any room for them I hasten to add. They were talking too about the fall of Zepa and how after four years they had been unable to continue defending the town and feared what had happened to Srebrenica some weeks before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, if I could ask you to slow down in your speech to give the translators an opportunity to stay with you. Now in talking to all of these people in these district locations, did they indicate to you similar stories about the shelling of Zepa which you briefly mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that the shelling had been relentless and they told me, and it was of interest to me professionally at the time, that a lot of the shelling was coming from within Serbia itself across the border. Zepa nestles against the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina on the River Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Once again what time frame was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking about shelling throughout the siege, from 1992 up until the fall of the town in 1995, but they were talking in particular about the recent shelling during the early summer which had led to the final collapse of the pocket. They were saying that, as far as they could ascertain, the gun positions from which they were being shelled were at a place called Jagodnica in Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If could you indicate where on the map that would be. That is Exhibit 181.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zepa and Jagodnica nestles against the border just here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is the border right on the other side of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jagodnica is not marked I am afraid but it is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To the west of Skarlarni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly equidistant between the two towns, just within the Serbian border. It is a high town on a hill, so I was told. I have not been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, the majority of the people that you talked to, were they civilians or were they military men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zenica they were civilians almost entirely, mostly women and children. The group in Dublin had all been in the army. My impression was that any male from the age of about 17 upwards in Zepa was in the army by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You indicated in your initial summary that the final instance of ethnic cleansing which you witnessed that stood out in your mind was your return to Travnik and the area of Vlasic. Can you describe for the Court what you encountered there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a wheel come full circle in its way. This was in August 1995 and I was back in Travnik. By then the Bosnian Army was pushing up towards Donji Vakuf held by the Serbs and to my surprise actually there were still small numbers of people coming into Travnik through that same crossing point at Smet, exactly as had been the case three years previous. This time they were in much smaller groups like 50 on one of the nights I went up to meet them. By now Travnik was so full there was no question of putting them up in town. They were by now being bussed up to tiny little mountain villages and put on the floors of schools up there. There were extraordinary scenes. There were families who had seen the lists of who was coming and were greeting relatives they had not seen for three years and so on. What I think was most interesting was the stories these people were telling, because they had been in Banja Luka and Prijedor for three years under the Bosnian Serb authorities and were telling the most, well, spine chilling tales. Some of them had lived in the cellars of their own homes, some of them had pretended to be Serbs or changed their name in order to get on, in order to sell produce at a market. Some of the men had been taken prisoner and sent out digging trenches for the Bosnian Serb side to use against their own people, because these were of course Muslims. Others had been in prison. Others had been in forced labour camps, factories. One man had worked in a railway yard. It was extraordinary to hear these stories coming from people who had walked that very same road. We talked of course about points on the road. The soldiers in Skender Vakuf, yes, well, I remember them, it was that sort of chat. The other extraordinary thing was I went back to the school gymnasium floor to which the people had come down off the mountains that day, that night that I travelled with them to find people that I knew from 1992 still there in the same place, same bit of floor. Their children had met other refugees. One couple had a baby by then. One old lady said -- some said they wanted to go home. One old lady said she never wanted to leave the gym; she had not been out of the gym for 18 months. As I knew, some told me, "Well, we are all going mad here really", but it was extraordinary to think that these people were still here three years later. People were still coming through and the people who come through with me three years earlier still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there also a reference to the massacre you mentioned earlier while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. With the by now advancing Bosnian Army I went up into their trenches where the mines were quite close, and it was extraordinary. I was able for the first time since 1992 to look down on Smet. Smet was the place where the cars were taken, where we set out in to the No Man's Land. We were looking down on the very spot and a man asked us to stop talking because it was August 21st and he said, "This is the third anniversary of the massacre at the ravine at Smet". Once again there was the sense of time going round in circles, but by now this massacre of which I had heard told when I returned to Travnik in September 1992 was a well-known thing. It had become famous throughout the army and throughout the country, throughout the world indeed. All the soldiers that I was with on that occasion were themselves, had been on that road. So there we were above Smet on the anniversary of the massacre, and all these men were themselves from Prijedor. Many of them had been in Omarska, in the camps. So by now everything was ringing very, very familiar indeed. Nothing much was changing, but known to us then the war was nearing an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What other aspects about the conflict that you experienced stand out in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the camps that I am describing, that I have mentioned above all -- you can come to those when you wish -- but also the opening up of the east of Bosnia, the Drina valley. This had been more or less sealed off during most of the war to almost all reporters. We had heard accounts of the violence there in the early months, but no-one had really been able to do any work there and to sustain what had been going on. That was one of the discoveries of the last few months that was particularly upsetting, and the siege of the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could start first with Eastern Bosnia? When did you begin your investigation in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soon after it became even partially safe to go there. People were, most people were working on Srebrenica and the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica, but I was more interested in places about which we knew almost nothing, but about which people, some refugees, were talking, namely, Visegrad and Foca, and especially Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could put on the map, Exhibit 181?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Visegrad is here on the River Drina just within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Foca -- follow the river down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What time frame is it that you are now looking in these areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was investigating these towns -- I never -- I should say, I became so wrapped up in Visegrad, I never actually got to Foca -- this was this year, earlier this year, in February and March '96.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you discover on your investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started to hear stories about the bridge at Visegrad. It is a famous bridge built by the Ottomans and the title of a book called "The Bridge on the Drina" by a writer called Ivo Andric, who is the only Yugoslav ever to win a Nobel Prize which he did for this book. So the bridge was a, sort of, symbol of Bosnia. I found out that the bridge had been used for very public mass executions of Muslims through a period of months in 1992. I first heard about this from one of the soldiers from Zepa in Dublin. He was 17 then and said he had been too young when he got to Zepa to join the army. He was from Visegrad and his job had been for three years to wade or sail a little boat out into the river in Zepa which is down river from Visegrad and to hoik corpses out of the water. He had done that for three years. I started to -- I just wanted to uncover this. I devoted a lot of energy into finding exactly what he was talking about. The people from Visegrad, there were 14,000 Muslims in Visegrad in 1992 and, unlike from the Prijedor/Banja Luka region in the places where the refugees tended to collect, Gorazde, in Sarajevo, they were pretty hard to find. There were not many of them around. But those who had been there in that spring to early summer 1992 all told the same story, whether they were in Ireland, Belgium, Holland, and various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the trucks would go down to this bridge and people would be shot and stabbed and bodies thrown into the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the victims ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- of these murders? Did these witnesses indicate to you who was committing these murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They said that it was a local gang of Bosnian Serbs and a name recurred which it would, perhaps, be inappropriate to mention at the moment. I am at your discretion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: They indicated that these murders were conducted in open on that bridge throughout the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Visegrad is rather like an arena. The town comes down two sides of a valley and the river runs through the bottom of the valley and the bridge spans the river. These executions took place nightly, if not daily. I spoke to people who had watched their families being executed on the bridge and their friends being executed on the bridge, people had survived, wounded in the water, shielded perhaps by other corpses from bullets, as was the case on one occasion. I managed to confirm a story which was that a manager of an hydroelectric power station further down river, across the Serbian border in Serbia itself, had made a phone call to the police station in Visegrad during this period, asking the police to relent on the killings because the corpses were blocking the calvets in his dam and to such a degree that he did not have the staff to remove them in time, and that the water was going over the dam instead of through the calvets. So it was clear to me from that sort of anecdote that this was killing on a very large scale indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you confirm that particular anecdote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got through to the power station and, albeit rather gruffly and briefly, the man on the end who identified himself as the manager -- to my translator -- said, "Da, da, da" -- "Yes, yes, yes" -- and put the phone down. But the other source for that was a testimony which I was given taken by the United Nations in Gorazde from a prisoner of the Muslim army, the Bosnian government in Gorazde, Serbian prisoner, who had talked in great detail about these killings on the bridge. He had also told this story having been -- and named the police officer who had taken the complaint and so on. I mean, it was documented in some detail from somebody from who had worked within the Visegrad police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there any estimation on the number of victims of these killings in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, as I was asked earlier, numbers is always a dangerous thing to do, but, I mean, we seemed to be talking about thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could turn now to Sarajevo. When did you first go to the capital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was first in Sarajevo in August 1992, about three to four months into the siege, on both sides of the line, both with the Serbs in the mountains above the city and with the completely mixed community of all three ethnic groups which was entrapped within the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of contact did you have with the Serbian forces that were surrounding the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given a rather good tour of gun positions and a splendid view of the city from above by two Serbian -- Bosnian-Serb soldiers based at Pale. This was during our inspection and visit to camps in the area. These two showed us the gun positions without any difficulty, without any embarrassment. I remember one remark one of them made when they were discussing the people down below, they said, "The only good Muslim is a dead Muslim", and he made, without actually firing, to sort of spray the city with bullets from his gun; and, yes, they did not make any -- they were not apologising for what they were doing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From the viewpoint of those gun positions, could you clearly see the various sections of the city below?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Sarajevo is in a bowl surrounded by mountains, so as you look down on the city it is almost like looking at a map. You can see the airport, you can see the main streets, you can see the various estates -- very clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you clearly see apartment buildings and homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you knew the city well enough, could you pick out where the hospital and other significant landmarks in the city were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I have to say no. This was early on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It was a general question, which was if you knew the city well enough ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, gosh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- could you do that from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I mean without binoculars, I mean, you could do that very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe, were you in the city itself when it was shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, frequently, on many occasions. It would be impossible to have been in the city when it was not being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe some of those specific instances that you were subject to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most infamous occasion that I was there for was the so-called water queue massacre of 1993, July, if I recall properly. The situation was a particularly pernicious one. Those laying siege to the city had cut off the gas and water at that time, and so people were being forced to go and queue for water in plastic cannisters or buckets at the very few points left in the city where you could still get it. One of those was a well in the fairly exposed suburb of Dobrinja near the airport and the No Man's Land. I was working down in the centre of the town when reports came through that a queue for water at this well had been shelled and there were large numbers of people killed. We got to the scene of the shelling, about between 10, maybe 20, minutes after these reports. The scene there was of bodies, bits of bodies. I remember the corporation workers who had by now attached hoses to the well, hosing sort of watery blood into the drainage. One thing I will not forget was this line of plastic cannisters where the people had been which were untouched in this sort of queue. It was like a sort of phantom queue for water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you able to determine whether the majority of the people in that line were civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were water queues all over Sarajevo at all times and invariably 98 per cent civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what -- if we can describe it as such -- would be a normal occasion of a shelling that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the shelling of Sarajevo was daily, nightly, if not hourly, sometimes minutely -- it is not a word I know -- but sometimes more than one shell would come into the same area within a minute. It is an extraordinary experience. You hear a sort of a whine in the air, followed by a loud thud, a sort of dead sound, and everything seems to be in slow motion. You hear shattering glass and people screaming and running and you run. This was something that I experienced a number of times. Other people, of course, lived with it for four years -- three years, forgive me. I remember one occasion when this happened and the shell came in. I was in a car at that time and the driver very quickly did a sort of very speedy U-turn away from the shell. People were running with us up the road away from the site of the shelling, and another shell came in not so far up the road in front of them in the area towards which they were running, suggesting a fairly sort of deliberate targeting of these missiles intended to cause maximum casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This group of people who were running, were they civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All civilian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there occasions when you could determine from where the fire was coming, the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the gun positions, as I knew from summer 1992, were up in the hills where the Serbian positions were, but the best time you could know for sure was at night, because when they were shelling at night, what they would do is often put up a flare and you could see that the flare was coming from the hills where the positions were. The flare would light the city and it was a most unwelcome sight, because within a short period of time of the flare hanging in the sky the shells would come smashing in, and that could be in the block next to you or right outside the hotel where we stayed at or it could be at the other end of the town, a distant thud. When they put a flare up, it would usually be they did not want to waste their flares. They used to put in quite a few shells. That was the time at which, I mean, it was beyond all doubt where they were coming from. There was also a lot of tracer fire in the darker hours which is a form of fire where one in every five bullets is lit so that the gunner can see his line, and you could see very clearly where that fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Again if you could please just slow down in your descriptions. If you could describe, please, the effect of these attacks on the people in the town that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the effects of the attacks on some people was obviously to kill them, on others to wound them and to cripple them. On those that the shells missed, it was to drive them slightly mad, for want of a better way of putting it. I remember a friend of mine saying once, "The thing about Sarajevo is that everybody in the city has a number on their back and you do not know what your number is, but it is between 1 and 300,000, and if 10 people are killed that day you know it is 11 upwards, but that you could be next". In Sarajevo, you are never out of range of the shells. A shell could hit you at any minute and during most of time you are walking around the streets you are within very easy sight of a sniper. It was extraordinary after the war to go into some of the snipers' nests, blocks of flats and so on, and to look through the holes that they had made and to see how easily they could see the streets, how easily identifiable the people were walking along them. So I think the idea was to, well, I cannot read the minds of those laying siege to the city, but the effect was, even to those who were not wounded or killed, that these people were going crazy with living on the edge of being attacked at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In August 1992, you were one of a group of journalists who were the first to visit the Omarska and Trnopolje camps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did that visit come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the month of July 1992, reports had been reaching the press and coming out in the -- and reaching the Croatian city of Karlovac in the testimonies of refugees that what was going on in the Prijedor and Banja Luka area was not just the intimidation and violence that we have described that led to people being desperate to leave the area or being deported from the area, but mass detentions in what were variously described as holding camps, holding centres, and so on. These were reported mostly in my own paper, The Guardian, by other people because during July 1992 I was still in London, and by a newspaper from New York called News Day and a reporter called Roy Gutman. Mr. Gutman published an article about a camp that he had located called Manjaca, which he described as being run by the Bosnian Serb military. A colleague of mine published a report towards the end of July in which people who had fled the area and were coming into the Croatian city of Karlovac were talking about a place called Omarska. The leader of the Bosnian Serbs, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, happened to be in London for a conference on, as I recall, 27th or 26th July. The Guardian had published that day an article on the front page in which people were talking about the word "Omarska" and a holding centre or a camp or some place called Omarska. Dr. Karadzic was on live television and he was cornered and questioned by the interviewer. He said that this was propaganda and that the -- I shall not try to repeat his exact words, they can be verified, but he gave to believe the accounts that were being given by people who had fled the area in Karlovac to the paper were untrue, and said to the interviewer on the television, which was a network called ITN, Independent Television News: "You know, if you insist, you can come and see for yourselves", I paraphrase. I cannot recall the exact words. Well, we insisted. The ITN said to him, either on air or soon after he went off air: "Well, we would like to take you up on that offer, if we may", and because The Guardian had carried the reports on this place, Omarska, we decided that we would join in and we would do it as a team effort and would take up the offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you leave for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I left the following day. My boss, the Foreign Editor, a man called Paul Webster, had a conversation with Dr. Karadzic by mobile phone as he was on his way to the airport and said: "We want to come, we want to look at this place". Dr. Karadzic said: "Well, you know, it will take a couple of weeks", and my boss, as I recall, said: "No, no, if that is all right with you, we will come straightaway. I have a reporter ready. We will be there tomorrow". I was told to organise myself to get to Belgrade via Budapest -- there was no flight to Belgrade -- to get there as soon as possible and to present myself, and that ITN would be doing the same thing. We met at the airport in Budapest in Hungary and drove to Belgrade. We arrived on 28th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you arrived in Belgrade, were there certain requirements that you had to accomplish first such as certifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had to accredit ourselves with an organisation called CRNA, C-R-N-A, which was the government press agency in Serbia. I mean, the project was in Bosnia but the accreditation was in Belgrade with the Serbian government press agency, CRNA, yes. I mean, we explained to them that we had come as Dr. Karadzic's, I will say "guests", although that is probably not quite the right word, and then they registered and gave us the necessary papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you given a point of contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were put under the tutelage of a woman called Klara Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What organisation was she from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She introduced herself as an officer of the Serbian Jewish Friendship Society which I found fairly confusing, frankly, but she seemed to be the woman in charge of at least the initial liaison with whatever authorities we were dealing with. It was never quite clear -- in Belgrade it was never quite clear. But she would be the person who would come to the Hyatt Hotel where we were staying and would relay to us what the plans were going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were met by her at the hotel did she have other individuals with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She came over quite a few times and there was a gathering organised by her at the hotel with various people. I could not quite work out what the purpose of it was, but one of them was the Vice President of the self-declared Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the Bosnian Serbs, Professor Nikola Koljevic, who was there. We talked generally about Serbian history and the suffering of the Serbs. They were telling us a lot about that and the present war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Longer than we had hoped. We were anxious to get on and to get to the Banja Luka/Prijedor area and get to Omarska, but we stayed there three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there an explanation for the delay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mainly, sort of, it was presented to us anyway as being bureaucratic, that everything had to be organised, it was difficult. There was a war on. There were logistical problems, "We are concerned for your security", that sort of thing. We, I think, had covered enough war by this time to know that, you know, we can look after ourselves, we just wanted to get on. They kept us there until our final departure date which was, as I recall, on August 2nd -- sorry, I think it was the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this period that you were in Belgrade, is that when you visited the Loznica camp which you have described earlier to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for want of a better way of putting it, we were killing time in Belgrade, and there was by then issued a list published by the Bosnian government of "concentration camps", and some of those locations were within striking range of Belgrade, day trip range of Belgrade, if you like, that would not lose us the opportunity to depart. Loznica was one of those. It, clearly, was not a concentration camp. My colleagues from ITN also made a visit to Subotica to find that that was not either. These were the transit camps that you saw on the video and I described earlier. So, yes, that was when I went down to Loznica. It is a short drive from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you finally travel to Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We travelled down to Pale which is the Bosnian Serb capital by military helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who arranged for the helicopter, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, as far as we were concerned, as far as we could see, it was Miss Klara Mandic of the Serbian Jewish Friendship Society, but, you know, one made one's own inferences. It did not seem that this organisation would necessarily have that much authority over military air transport, and the place from which we left was a place under the authority of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Pale, what was the first event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a helicopter landed in a field, took off again and before long we were introduced to Dr. Karadzic, the President of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could play the tape, please? Do you recognise what this is, if you put it on the video monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is me on the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During that helicopter ride what did you notice? If you could stop the tape for a moment, please? What could you see out of the windows of the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We flew over Eastern Bosnia and were able to see village after village destroyed. When I say "destroyed", I mean completely destroyed, every house destroyed, empty, not even any soldiers, not like Zepa as I described earlier, but just sort of ghost villages smashed to pieces. I remember looking down at them and looking at the soldier who was with us on the helicopter and an expression of rather morbid, yes, pleasure on his face. I wrote, I think, somewhere that it looked as though he was savouring some sort of gastronomic delicacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could play the tape again, please, with the audio again? I would recommend the headphones for the court. This is approximately a 10 minute section.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 184, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes 184, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could stop the tape there for a moment, please? Later in your journey, in fact, upon your arrival in the area of the camps, was there an incident of an attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did it, in fact, turn out to be a real attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We thought at the time, and I am even more convinced now, that the apparent attack on us, on our convoy as we went towards Omarska, was a fake. We were approaching the camp and suddenly there was some shooting just over us from out of the woods, and the people who were with us, the Bosnian Serb police who were escorting us, jumped out of their amoured personnel carrier. They were running around on a bridge and getting into the ditch and there was quite an exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is this shown later on in the video tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could continue the tape now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: if you could stop the tape, please? That would be a convenient place to break?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for lunch until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you like to continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Vulliamy, after the brief interview with Radovan Karadzic, what was next on the agenda in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lunch. We were asked into his headquarters for a meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who presided over this lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man who took charge of us generally then and presided over the lunch was the Vice President of the Bosnian Serbs, Professor Nikola Koljevic, whom we had met before in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who else made appearances at that lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the building at the same time, it was pointed out to us a Mr. Krajisnik who was an official in the parliament there in Pale, and a swashbuckling figure came past and was very briefly introduced as the military Commander. I now know that to have been General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After lunch did you then travel to one of the camps which the Bosnian Serbs wanted you to visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Which camp was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to a camp or prison on the outskirts of Sarajevo in the Serb held area called Kula. This was in a part of the city called Lukavica under the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could roll the next sections of the video, please, without any audio. Exhibit 184. Is that the Kula camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this looks like Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This was the camp which Dr. Karadzic had referred to in his interview which we listened to, where he said people who had committed homicide against Serbs were being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. This is the same place as the one he wanted us to see and the one whose inmates he had previously described as people who were suspected of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you speak to some of these inmates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, both in the presence of the guards and for a very brief period alone with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did they indicate was the reason they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as their testimonies went, there was certainly nothing to do with homicide or murder. They were civilians from two suburbs of Sarajevo, Hadzici and another. They had been taken from their homes to another place where they said they had been brutally treated by extremists and thereafter taken by the Bosnian Serb military to this place, Kula, where they said the treatment was slightly better. They said they did not know why they were, but they were waiting for exchange in return for Serbian people who had been taken by the other side. In our discussions afterwards, we decided that they were a sort of currency of the war, a human currency. Their story was that they were just civilians who had been rounded up and herded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you finally begin your journey to the Prijedor opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning. We stayed overnight in Pale, the Bosnian Serb capital, and then after a wait we were boarded on to a military sort of mini bus and taken north from Pale to the town of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could utilize the map, Exhibit 181, and point out the route which you travelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is Pale and we are travelling up here, up here, through here to Bijeljina where we take a break; and then we carry on through what is called the corridor, Brcko, a series of dirt tracks through this narrow stretch of land held by the Serbs here, through Derventa and thence to Banja Luka. There is Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe some of what you saw along that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, two very different sorts of community, if I may say so. One, intact, normal places, people going about their normal lives and, in other parts, areas of widespread and wholesale destruction, by which I mean buildings burned out, buildings blown up, buildings strafed with machine gunfire, either stretched out along the road. In the rural areas or sometimes concentrated in urban settlements where, well, almost every building you could see in some parts were destroyed. I mean, this was the case in the town of Brcko which we went through in that corridor that I pointed out earlier. So, there would be some communities intact, other communities partially, if not wholly, destroyed and the destroyed ones empty of people, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You remained overnight in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The following day how did you travel to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were met at the hotel to which they took us by a man introducing himself as Major Milutinovic who said he was responsible for liaison on behalf of the Bosnian-Serb army in Banja Luka. We went in the same vehicle with him -- hang on, no, the vehicle came up behind. Forgive me. We went in a car -- I cannot remember whose car it was -- to Prijedor that morning with him through a very different landscape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was different about the landscape there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for at least the second half of the journey virtually every house that we passed on the side of the road, be it alone or in a collection of houses, had been blown up, burned down, strafed with fire, or all three, and we were skirting the town at that point or at one point along the way of Kozarac before arriving in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the scene in Kozarac as you went by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The centre of the town was a little way off to our right, that is, to the north of the road we were taking. We were looking up the hill at it and, more immediately, at the houses beside the road down which we were driving which were the outskirts of the town. Almost every building, as I say, was destroyed, burned, shelled, the roof burned off, charred, signs of fire, both artillery and machine gunfire, against the walls. Every now and then, surreally, would be a house intact, either intact and unattended, or sometimes even intact and with people going about their business in the garden or hanging up some washing or something like that. There were also in some of the fields of the uninhabited areas people tending the fields as we were getting towards harvest time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask Major Milutinovic about these people that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We said: "Who are the people in the fields?" and we asked him about the houses too. He said: "The people in the fields" -- well, he answered variously. He said that some were Muslims and Croats who had had, and I quote, "accepted the new order" and that others were Serbs; that was the people working in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the next segment of the video, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What did he say about the buildings? Was it a two-part question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry. I must be hearing something. You asked him about the housing too. He said people in the field. What did he say about the housing? MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Did you ask him about the disparity between the houses which were completely intact and those which were destroyed right next to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to be sort of delicate about it. We were very much under his command, as it were. The aim was to get to the camp so we tried to be as tactful as possible. I remember asking: "So whose are the intact houses?" He did not say anything and I said: "Are they the Serbs?" He sort of grunted in a way that I took to mean affirmative, sort of the "Hmmm", like that. He then was telling us all the while about how 40,000 refugees had left the area. At that point I did not see any reason to push him on it. We wanted to get to the camp rather than engage in a confrontation over who had or had not left the area. At that point it did not seem politic or in my interests to engage him in an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the tape now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Continue. Are these following scenes representative of the type of destruction that you saw all along the trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the sort of thing. These houses are actually in better condition than some of those we saw. I mean, the walls are in the main still standing. I mean, a lot of them had been destroyed completely -- more like that one that has just gone past. Yes, there is a typical one. Yes, this is the sort of thing. I mean, it went on for miles and miles and miles, both at Kozarac and in many communities preceding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion with the escorts as you were driving by these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before meeting Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we asked the soldiers as we went through the town of Brcko, which was a particularly, you know, extensively destroyed place, "What is all this? What has been happening here? What happened to this place?" because that really was a landscape to behold. They said: "Oh, this is a Serbian town. This has been done by the Croats in the fighting". At that time I did not know enough to disagree; were he to say the same to me now, I would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could continue with the next segment, please? Is this a representation of the effect you were talking about with having houses standing next to each other, some totally destroyed while others in perfect condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a representation of the proximity of them, yes. In some places it was even more bizarre than that. You would have great rows of destroyed buildings and then maybe sort of one in the middle intact and inhabited. I drove down the same road just earlier on this year and that is still the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You can stop the tape now. You indicated in the earlier answer that Major Milutinovic had referred to the fact that there had been 40,000 displaced persons. Did he make any particular references to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did talk about Kozarac. He talked about it as a place that had seen considerable violence during the Second World War, and its proximity to the concentration camp which was kept by the pro-Nazi Croatian regime at that time in which the enemies of that regime were kept and in turn detained and killed in large numbers. Kozarac had been one of the assembly points for taking people to that camp, he explained to us, and that was -- he did not say much more; he just said that "large numbers of Serbs were killed around here in Jasenovac which is just over there, and a lot of them came from Kozarac". Jasenovac was a place familiar to me. I had been there during my coverage of the Croatian war and I knew it to be a place where large numbers of Serbs and also Muslim and Croat dissidents under that regime, Jews and gypsies had been killed and detained in large numbers; so I knew what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask the Major about the camps which you wanted to visit while you were driving around

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked about that more than anything else and continued to say that "We hoped we were going to Omarska. Omarska is where we have asked to go. That is what Dr. Karadzic has said that we would be able to do", and he kept saying: "Well, I want you to see somewhere called Manjaca. That will be much more interesting for you", he said, "and, as a soldier, I can help you get access to it. That is the place I think you will go to", and it was clearly the place he wanted to take us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you arrived in Prijedor, what was the first significant event that made an impression on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We parked in the centre of the town outside the Civic Centre, the Town Hall, and the first thing I saw was a long queue of women down the side of one of the streets just outside the -- adjacent to the Civic Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can we run the video tape, please? Is that the queue of women you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to talk to those women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why did they tell you they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We talked to them both while we were waiting for our appointment inside and again afterwards. On both occasions they said more or less the same thing. They said that this office they were queuing up outside, although it was in the police station, was a refugee office, and that they were being told that they could, at a price, leave. They had diverse accounts of whether or not they wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Stop the tape, please. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said variously whether they wanted to leave or not, but the thing that they were most concerned about, and the one thing that they all had in common, was that their husbands and men folk or older sons had been taken away from them and their homes, and they did not know where they were. They were trying to get information off this police station/refugee office -- it seemed to be the same thing -- as to where their men folk might be. The word that was going around between them and that they conveyed to us was Omarska, and that made us more determined to get where we hoped we were heading for. There were at that time the first accounts that I heard direct of people talking about violence against their homes and firing guns into their houses, but -- it sounds callous now but I will say it -- we were so impatient to get on with our trip to the camp that one paid now, perhaps not forgivably, rather scant regard to this, took it on board but did not bother to make a big thing of it; we just wanted to get on with the day's programme. The most interesting thing that they said to us, therefore, was that they had heard about Omarska and this is where they believed their men folk were and had been for some weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you got inside the building who did you first meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went through various rigmarole downstairs, and then we were taken up to a room to meet a group of men ready to hold some sort of conference for us. The first man we were introduced to was the Chief of Police. He was introduced as a man called Simo Drljaca. He through -- he had an interpretress whose name was Nada Balaban, and the introductions duly made to a Colonel called Vladimir Arsic, introduced to us as the Commander for the military in the region, and then two other principal civilian -- I took it they were civilian; they were described as civilian officials although they were in military uniform -- the President of what was described to us as the Crisis Committee or Crisis Staff, a man called Milomir Stakic, and another man who was described as his Deputy, Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the next segment of the video tape, please? (Video tape played) Who was that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man just passed then on the left is Dr. Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man is the Colonel, Vladimir Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man is Milomir Stakic and he was the President of the Crisis Staff and also the Mayor of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could stop the tape, please. Did you have in this meeting an opportunity to hear each one of these men speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who began the meeting for that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting was begun, well, as it were, the pleasantries were begun by the police chief, Mr. Drljaca, but the main, sort of, the man who kicked off the meeting, as it were, was Colonel Arsic of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He made a long speech. It was a long meeting -- longer than we really wanted. He gave a long speech, the gist of which was that he would like us to visit a camp called Manjaca which, as Commander of the military in the area, he had authority to take us to because it was a military camp for prisoners of war, he said. We said variously, I mean, it was a speech into which we interjected and saying, "We want to go to Omarska", and he said, "No, Manjaca will be much more interesting for you because in Manjaca you have real Muslim fighters and prisoners of war, but in Omarska you only have civilian refugees". The more he went on in this way, the more determined we were, of course, to go to Omarska. One of the things that he said was that, you know, that there was a, sort of, processing going on in Manjaca, and described impending hearings for these prisoners of war to determine who was guilty and who was not. Now, I should say the thing about Manjaca, I mean, you might think we were, sort of, looking a gift horse in the mouth, but Manjaca had already been inspected by the International Red Cross. We knew this and that, as it were, you know, that had been done and, professionally speaking, because I was there doing a job rather than preparing for this. Manjaca had also been visited by Mr. Roy Gutman of the New York News Day, newspaper. If you will forgive a calculated professional judgment, it was not something that we wanted to do, to go to a camp that had already been, if you will pardon the expression, "done" by somebody else. Omarska was the place everyone was talking about; Omarska was the place that we had got on the trail of; Omarska was what the women were talking about, and this exchange with Colonel Arsic went on for a while, to and fro. He gave us a bit of background on what had happened in the area which was more fully explained later, but at the end of this conversation he said that he did not have authority to take us to Omarska anyway, because Omarska was not run by the military, and we would have to ask elsewhere for permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Milomir Stakic then enter into the discussion with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Stakic came in briefly, and made his main speech later on but, as it transpired, the people to whom we would appropriately apply to go to Omarska who were in charge of Omarska, ergo, had the authority to take us there, were indeed sitting in the room. They were Mr. Stakic, the Mayor of Prijedor, his Deputy, Mr. Kovacevic, and the police chief. So we said: "Well, we will ask these people then if we can go there instead of you, Colonel. Thank you for your help but, obviously, you are not in a position; maybe these people are". Mr. Stakic then embarked on a long account of what, according to him, had been happening in the area. He said that he had tried to make peace with the Muslims but that they had refused his offers of peace. He said that they had documentation on the distribution of, if I remember rightly, 3,500 weapons or, sorry, weapons to 3,500 Muslim men in the village of Kozarac. He said that the local Muslims were being whipped up by extremists who had come in from outside. The tenor was, you know, "We want peace with these people but they do not want peace. They are preparing for some sort of insurrection". Our request to go to Omarska under his authority, rather than to have this conversation about what was going on in the area, seemed to have got lost in his monologue at this point. I cannot remember how the conversation fizzled out, but we then -- it turned into a sort of round robin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him specifically about the camps and who was in the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that -- I mean, he would not use the word "camps"; he kept saying "transit centres", "centre", "centres", "There are not any camps, there are only centres". He seemed to echo -- actually, it got confusing and it is confusing now, it was confusing then; whereas the Colonel had said: "Omarska is boring, you will not want to go there, it is just civilians", it was either Mr. Stakic or his colleague, Kovacevic, who at this point said: "Oh, there are prisoners of war in Omarska. There are people being screened as to whether or not they are in the army". We were (and, if you will pardon me for being illogical, it was an illogical conversation), we were going round and round and it was becoming unclear as to whether whoever was in Omarska was being screened for being in the army or was a civilian refugee; it depended on who you talked to. It also depended on who you talked to in the room whether it was being called a "camp" or a "centre" or a "transit holding point" or something, but, of course, all this was happening through translators, so the semantics are difficult. But, either way, you know, we were getting impatient, I was getting impatient. We were getting nowhere. All that was becoming clear was that Manjaca OK, Omarska not OK; and the more the conversation went that way, the more determined we were to go to Omarska, the more we insisted that we must.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kovacevic enter into the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kovacevic was introduced as the man in charge of the camp in terms of its day-to-day running, along with the police chief. He opened up by saying, fairly frankly: "Well, I do not actually want you here anyway", or some such word. He said: "I do not approve of your presence here", and he gave two reasons for that; one was, as I recall, he said: "I have had a bad experience with the international mass media", and he said that he feared for our security if we went to Omarska. The security question took us by surprise, I remember it taking me by surprise, because every time we talked about Manjaca or anything else, there did not seem to be a security problem, but there always was a security problem whenever we talked about Omarska. Dr. Kovacevic then ------

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he, as it were, did his turn and he told us that there was not anything that people like us could tell the Serbs about concentration camps because he himself had been born in one. I found this quite interesting, that here is the man who is introduced as running this camp and it turns out he was born in a camp. I asked him about it, and he said that he been born in Jasenovac which was the camp kept by the Croats in the previous generation. This was taken as a -- he talked a bit about the war. He made, retrospectively, a rather ironic point, that it was some time before the outside world knew about the concentration camps kept by the Nazis and even longer before they did anything about it. So I was quite interested -- I was waking up a bit at this point and more interested in this sort of conversation because this man's mind was clearly quite an interesting one, from a professional point of view. However, we were not getting very far in our request. I believe at this point Mr. Stakic came back in and said that he wanted to show us a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the video supposed to be about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stakic's points thus far had been Islamic insurrection. As I said before, the 3,500 armed men, the Serbs seeking to defend themselves and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had Dr. Kovacevic made any references to crimes or atrocities committed against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned one place in which he said 20 Serbs had been killed by Muslim gunmen. Some were outside Prijedor. I do not recall the name of the village. He had also, I should say, been getting out maps at various points during this conversation, and said something quite interesting. He said -- he got out a map that had been devised in 1941 showing the greater Serbia -- we touched on that a bit yesterday, this was the occasion I was thinking of -- and got out this map showing great tranches of land which was called "Serbia" and said to us, in an odd twist in the conversation, I remember he said: "You are lucky to be here at this great moment in the history of the Serbs". I thought it was a curious, rather flamboyant remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he make reference to evidence or instances of Serbian babies being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There was a line, during the depiction of this so-called Islamic uprising, he said that (and I wrote this one down) that the River Una, which runs along the edge of the Bihac pocket, there had been, quote, "hundreds of Serbian babies nailed to crosses with their eyes gouged out". Dr. Karadzic had told us yesterday that hundreds of Serbian babies had been found nailed to crosses with their eyes gouged out floating down the Drina river on the other side of the country, so there was an allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In this video was there any proof of these atrocities or these preparations for battle which they had talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
