utterances.text: Well, the video that they showed started with a fact that a copy of the Koran had been found in somebody's house, and then it went on to show a casket of ammunition being opened up with lots of bullets and a sort of bandaliero type thing inside, and there were various shots of soldiers, but I do not remember it very well. I have to confess, I rather lost interest in the video. There was a commentary which was itself rather like a machine gun, and the thing was being variously interpreted. I just remember hearing words like "jihad" and things, and I was not -- I confess, I was not paying a great deal of attention after the first five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the rest of that video segment, please, with the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Stop the video, please. How did the meeting end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting went on for quite a long while after the video, and it ended with us saying: "Look, it is Omarska", and I think we made it clear that we were not going to leave until we had been to this place and could we, please, sort of hurry up and get there. We were told to go outside and to wait outside on the street while they talked in private, which we did. We carried on our interviews with the women on the pavement actually at that time. This lasted about 20 minutes. After a while, Mr. Drljaca, the police chief, came out of the civic centre and said: "Come on, we are going, we are going Omarska", and we organised our vehicles ready for take off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did anyone attempt to join your group at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to my professional annoyance, a car with British number plates arrived with a colleague of mine called Tim Juda(?) from The Times at the wheel and a colleague, another colleague from the French paper, Liberation. "Hello, Tim", "Hello, Ed", usual sort of thing. "What are you doing?" "Well, we are hoping to get to Omarska actually". "Oh, really, do you mind if we come along?" The sort of public answer, as always, was, "No, not at all, please do"; the private answer was, "Dam!" So they joined our convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were they allowed to stay in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately for them, they were not. I would rather you did not ask my view on that. The police came up to them and said: "Who are you? What are you doing?" They said: "Well, apparently, these people are going to go to Omarska; we would like to come too". They were asked by the police: "Well, are you part of this" -- they went into another conclave, came out again, away again, said: "Are you part of Dr. Karadzic's invitation?" They said no, and then the police told them to get out of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After that did the convoy proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we set off finally out of the town of Prijedor back along the road that we had taken into the town towards Omarska. We had seen the turn off to Omarska on the way and now we were going back towards it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have an armed escort with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We were in our bus. There was a car in front of us and a blue painted amoured personnel carrier with a turret machine gun thing on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the next segment of the video tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As you were travelling to the camp, you made reference earlier to a battle scene which occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately how long into the trip had that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall, but it was after we turned off the main road, so it must have been about 20 minutes or so, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is this the scenes of that battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is, indeed, the scene. What happened was there was shooting, bullets came quite close over us and, well, I do not need to describe it. You can see men rushing about. To our right here off camera is a man crouching in a ditch firing. The amoured personnel carrier was also firing quite dramatically into the woods. This chap seems to be standing around. He is not very worried. Anyway, it was an exchange of fire that lasted quite a time. I mean, it was -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Stop the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a pretty -- an apparently serious one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did this battle end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did this battle end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It ended because Major Milutinovic was saying: "It is not safe for you". He said, I remember him saying, "They shoot journalists around here, you know". He said: "It is not safe for you. The Muslims are in the woods". He said: "There are mujaheddin in the woods and we cannot go any further". We sort of took stock amongst ourselves. One of us was quite worried and thought, well, maybe there are Muslims in the woods and maybe they will shoot us but, as is more likely the case, even if this is a fake, this is quite a good get out for them, quote, you know, "The Muslim gunmen shot the journalists". That was probably quite a good point, given what Dr. Karadzic had said the previous day about, you know, you may be attacked and concerns for our safety and so on. I am afraid I was not being very sort of judicious at this point. I was just so sort of cross and anxious to get on with it and fed up with all this messing about, and I conferred with another colleague. We just said: "Look, this is ridiculous. There is no war going on around here. We have been driving around this place for nearly 24 hours now. We have not heard a single shot. Now suddenly there is a battle going on outside the place we want to go to. This is rubbish. This is a prank". I got quite angry with Major Milutinovic. I said: "No, we will carry on, if you please. We insist. This is nonsense. Can we keep going?" and then the battle abruptly stopped and we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you can slow down just a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I said: "Can we stop this prank and continue?" and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know now at this time at the scene of that battle site how far you actually were from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was hard to tell -- I am sorry, I should have mentioned this earlier. We went down the main road, past the turn off to Omarska. "Oh, dear", heart sink, perhaps we are not going there after all that. We instead take another turn off further on down the road to the right and wind through all sorts of dusty tracks and back roads, thinking, well, whatever is on the direct road to Omarska, which I know now to be about 90 seconds drive from the turn off, they do not want us to see. We drove instead through these, as I say, tracks and back roads which were in themselves very interesting, because there were large numbers of burned and blown out houses of the kind you have seen all around that back area and equally large numbers of houses with white sheets sometimes hanging from the trees, white pillow cases, white flags flying. We asked Mr. Milutinovic what these were, and he said that these were -- oh, yes, yesterday we had seen them and he said they were Muslims and Croats who had accepted the new order. Today he said they were people waiting to leave. So, yes, we -- I am sorry, we went up a back route, a long back route, it emerged, to avoid going in through the front gate of the Omarska iron ore mining complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could show the next segment of the tape, please? Is this the entrance of the convoy into the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is us going in the back gate of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could stop the tape right there, please, with the picture? Who is the man on the left in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man on the left is Major Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The man in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man in the middle is the police chief, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The man on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man on the right was introduced to us as the Commander on the ground in the camp, a Mr. Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this point what is occurring when you first arrive in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what is occurring is what we sort of feared would be another set of hurdles. There was a conversation about whether we can talk to the prisoners and Mrs. Balaban, not in the picture translating what one of them was saying, I do not know which, said that "none of these prisoners want to talk to you". We had not actually asked any of them; we had not seen any yet. But, initially, the briefing was: "They do not want to talk to you", and that is what I can remember from that bit of the conversation anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you first go in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went around the corner of the building you can see on the screen, into a sort of yard area beyond that building looking towards the main bit of the complex. We could see the buildings that make up the complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What part of the camp did you actually go into first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we stayed outside for a while and watched a group of men being, well, if I can describe this, they were coming up in front of us across the yard. This is before we went into the building. There was a large, rusty red coloured hangar, a sort of large shed. There were other buildings around but this was the biggest one. From the other side of the yard, we could see a group of men emerging out of the door in the side of this hangar, and they were sort of, quite obviously, adjusting to the light -- it was bright sunlight and hot -- and they were lined up by men with guns into formation. There was a building to our left which is the one you seen on the video. This building is over the other side of the yard. They were made to jog in an obviously rehearsed camp drill across the yard, drilled by the men with the guns, and watched from above, from the top of the building we saw in the video, by a beefy machine gunner with a big gun on a tripod, a pair of reflective sunglasses, I remember. He was in a sort of position with a window, and he followed them with the gun as they made this fairly wretched jog in line across the yard into the building beside which we were standing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I had a question when the last video was being shown, but I did not want to interrupt you, Mr. Keegan. But there was a gentleman standing there with a beret on. He was the furthest one from at least our views. Do you recall what colour that beret was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, it was a sort of reddish colour, maroon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You will see it on the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I cannot wait, is that what you are telling me? Hold on -- OK, I will. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): From there did you go into the canteen area of that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could we run the tape again, please? Pick it up where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Continue to run. Is this the view inside the canteen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the inside of the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was your first impression when you saw these men eating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when they were running across the -- when they had been running across the yard, I could see that some of them, at least, were in the most appalling condition. They were very thin, others in reasonable condition, others skeletal. When they were eating, they were eating like -- well, we will see it -- they were eating fairly avidly. They were eating as though they had not eaten for a very long time, as though they had not seen food for a while. It was a fairly sobering sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you able to interview many of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, we tried -- that is the television crew doing so there. They were under the watchful eyes of the guards who were patrolling the canteen. We tried to talk to them as best we could. They were reluctant to do so. The physical state of some of them told us more than their words, quite honestly, as to what kind of treatment they were getting. One boy did talk about how he had been arrested, but there was very little to go on in terms of interviews and words. They were manifestly scared -- scared stiff actually. One of them did say something which I will never forget. He simply said: "I do not want to tell any lies but I cannot tell the truth".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately how long was your group allowed to remain in the canteen area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in the canteen area for three lunch shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were given a minute to eat each -- each shift was given a minute to eat this bowl of watery bean stew and half a roll, and most of them -- they were then lined up. They were called to order and they could get back in line and, as you see here, they were then marched out of the building as the next lot came in. A large number of them, I noticed, were keeping their roll or part of the roll for later. I remember writing that if they were eating even half that much every day they would not be quite so thin and hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could stop the tape, please? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you saw the pictures. They were -- they looked malnourished, their eyes were -- the worst of them, this is -- eyes bulging. You asked if we could interview them. The answer is, on the understanding of the word "interview" that I am used to, no, we could not. It sounds stupid to say, but I am going to say it, that the stares that they gave us told us more than what they told us. I mean, there is something inimitable about somebody staring at you in that way that is saying, "You know, look at me, and try to work out for yourself what I am trying to say". If that sounds like gilding the lily, it is not, because that was the atmosphere in that place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From the canteen where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we asked to see the sleeping quarters and we had heard there was a medical centre. We wanted to see that. They said: "No, we are going upstairs now" and, to my disappointment, we find ourselves in an office and we said: "Are we going to see the sleeping quarters? Can we see where these people are living and can we go into this hangar?" I mean, it was the red building from which these men had emerged in these three shifts that was, obviously, of interest. That was, you know, that was where our journey clearly had to end. But they said: "No, we are going to an office now for a briefing", and we then went upstairs above to the floor above the canteen in the same building for a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the video tape with the audio this time, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could stop the tape, please? In addition to the discussion about the various categories of prisoners in the camp, did you ask questions regarding whether international organisations such as the Red Cross had been allowed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew that the International Red Cross had not been allowed in, but I asked, had the International Red Cross been allowed in. The reply from Mr. Drljaca was that, "We would like to have the International Red Cross in because it is so expensive to have this place". I did not quite understand that. Mrs. Balaban then added either her own comment or was translating somebody else's remark, I do not recall whose, saying: "No, we do not need the Red Cross in here because this is not a camp, it is a centre", so I was no wiser than when I began asking the questions. I was also asking over and over again: "Can we see the sleeping quarters, please?" to which there was no quick response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What occurred as you left the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We finally left the office and Mr. Drljaca, or one of his people with him, I cannot remember who, said: "We would like you to interview the leader of the local Muslim party, the SDA, now", and they presented a man in the corridor. Well, to be honest with you, I just wanted to get on and see these sleeping quarters. I just wanted to get into the shed. I did not want to sit around and interview somebody that they had suggested I interview. This was all time, these were all hurdles now. We had had taste enough from the canteen as to what kind of "interviews" these were going to be, if any. I did not want to talk to anybody from a political party in a corridor surrounded by guards. This was not going to get us anywhere in particular, I thought. "No, thank you". We declined the invitation to interview this man and said: "Come on, let us go and have a look in the hangar, please".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any other news agencies besides the ITN crews who accompanied you on this trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, I should have said this at the beginning. Back in Pale, we had been joined by a television crew from the Bosnian Serb television channel who were making a film of us visiting Omarska. I did not actually take much notice of them. Most of the time I forgot they were there until a rather bizarre episode in the office. Sorry to return to the office, but in the office there was another exchange of fire in the woods. They said: "Oh, it is the Muslims in the woods shooting again", but paid no heed. We said: "Oh, enough of this nonsense", but the Bosnian Serb TV then did an interview with Mr. Drljaca saying: "Are we safe? Who are these people in the woods?" He was saying: "It is the Muslims in the woods". That was the only time I noticed them, but they were with us, yes, throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you get outside what transpired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a discussion about going into the hangar and seeing the rest of the camp which then developed into something of an argument, because they seemed to be saying that our visit had come to an end, and we were saying: "But Dr. Karadzic had said that we could see whatever we wanted", and they said, well, you know, they said various things. One of the things was that we were not safe in the camp. Mrs. Balaban said something that I found particularly interesting. When we challenged her on Dr. Karadzic's promise that we could see whatever we wanted, she said something to the effect of: "He told us you could see this and this, but not that", suggesting that there had been some instruction from him as to what we could or could not see within the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can we see the next part of the video tape, please, with the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could stop the tape, please? Was that the end of your visit in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was almost the end of the visit. Just after that, the gentleman you see in the flack jacket, Ian Williams of ITN, and I, I said: "Come on, Ian, let us just walk over there and see what happens". We took a few paces and the two gentlemen, Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Mejakic, you see retreating, then sort of moved around in an arc as though to block us, and I felt, perhaps, there was a line being drawn by that manoeuvre that was not worth crossing. In the exchange, one of the bits that gets slightly lost was Mr. Drljaca saying that we are not safe here; whereas that had previously applied to the supposed Muslims in the woods, one sort of began to wonder where the threat might come from if we pushed it. Then that was it. I have just remembered something pertaining to interviews in the canteen; would be it be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. I have suddenly remembered something, looking at the film. I did an interview which is not on the camera with a man who had a wound down the side of his face. I said: "Where did you get that from?" He said: "Oh, I fell over", and I remember going, "Fell over?" I met this man on a frontline when he was a soldier three years later. It was an extraordinary moment. He said: "I know you". I said: "I am sorry, I do not remember you", because he had doubled in weight by then. He said: "Do you remember when you were in Omarska there was a man with a wound to the side of his face who said he had fallen over?" I said: "Yes, of course I remember him". He said: "That was me". He said: "Well, no, I was lying. There was a guard just behind you. I hoped you would believe me. I think the lady from the television believed me". It was, sort of, just, sorry, to round up that point about not being able to do interviews. It was an extraordinary moment having this man recognise me, and we talked about a lot about what had happened since, but perhaps just in parenthesis I remembered that, watching the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the group do next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We abandoned our attempt to get into the shed for the reason I have just explained, and we got back in our bus and went to Trnopolje camp, again through the same sort of landscape that I have described before of destroyed houses and some intact houses with white sheets and pillow cases flying from the windows or trees.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you move on to that camp, you indicated earlier in your testimony that Roy Gutman from News Day had discovered Omarska. I gather that was before this trip that we have just seen, your trip, is that correct? Then I wanted to know whether they had gotten or he had gotten into the camp Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry if that was not clear. What had happened precedent to that visit was that Mr. Gutman had heard about a camp called Manjaca, which was the military camp that they were trying to get us to go to see. He had a couple of days before our visit, that was August 5th, on August 2nd he had published a story from inside Manjaca. He had also talked to refugees from the Prijedor region in Croatia who were talking about Omarska, and had also interviewed some people who had been in Omarska, but he had not been in the camp. So he had been writing about Omarska. My colleague, a woman called Maggie O'Kane of The Guardian had also been writing about Omarska based on a mixture of, in Maggie's case, people from the area who had heard about it, much like the women in the streets in Prijedor but who had got out. Mr. Gutman had found some people who had been in the camp and had interviewed them in, I believe, Croatia but I am not sure exactly where. But nobody had been inside the camp before that day. It had been mentioned on the basis of testimony but not visited by anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were your first impressions when you reached Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, we pulled up across a scrap of land from this scene here -- can I switch this off? I will describe it better if I am not looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We pulled up across a patch of land from a remarkable scene. I remember thinking, this does not belong in this time. I have no idea who was more amazed to see who, us, the people that were standing behind this barbed wire fence, or them to see a bunch of people with notebooks and television camera getting out of a bus. We walked across the stretch of land towards them. We shook hands with some of them. It was bewildering. I am going to describe who was behind the wire with the video off because I can do it better if I am not trying to accompany the picture. Some of them were in what might be described as "normal" condition, others were in appalling condition ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- skeletal and malnourished and standing up behind this barbed wired fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you get the opportunity to talk to some of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask them where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had come from all over the place. The man that I started talking to first whose emaciated figure then became known throughout the world as a result of these pictures, his name was Fikret Alic and he was from Kozarac and he had, you know, we were now -- our heads were full of Omarska and now here we were in this other place. I said: "Were you in Omarska or have you been here, or what have you been doing?" He said: "No, I was in another place call Keraterm". Here was a name I had not heard before. I said: "Good Lord, well, what is Keraterm like?" He said: "Well, it is much worse than here". He told the story about how he had been, well, he said that about 200 people were killed in one night there, and his friend who had also been in Keraterm said that Omarska was even worse, and they had come from Keraterm that morning, said Mr. Alic, the thin, the very thin man. That was quite a long conversation with him. He had some friends with him, as I said, who were also in Keraterm who told the same sort of story. I said: "200 people in one night? How do you know?" He said: "I know because I was there" and -- well, to be honest one went on a kind of over-drive at this point. I mean, one was writing down as, you know, bits that were coming, that people were saying, and conducting interviews as methodically as one could in the circumstances when confronted with this sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you then guided around the camp by a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was surprisingly easy at Trnopolje to give the guards the slip after what had happened in Omarska, and there was one man there -- his name was Ibrahim, and he sort of whisked me away and said: "Come on, you know, you can come inside", and so I followed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did he tell you about the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, yes, he did, and showed me around the inside. It was a school, Trnopolje, a school and its grounds, and he said: "Everything happens here". I said: "Is it as bad as Omarska?" He said: "No, no, no, it is nothing like Omarska, but there is violence and there is beating", and he said something, he said: "And they give the women a hard time". I think we touched on this theme yesterday. One was so sort of dazed concentrating on, trying to concentrate on one thing at a time, that I let that slip by, and even the women in our party who had similar things did not sort of latch on to this thing of rape that we were actually being told about, but we were talking about conditions, beating. We wanted to anchor this thing down somehow. But Ibrahim told me that people were coming here from other camps, that they were coming here from villages. In the grounds of the school, we sat, I sat down and, using him as an interpreter, although his English was not great, it was OK, started to talk to families that were encamped out in this heat, in this crowded place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he describe how the conditions in the camp compared to the conditions out in the town, in some of the local communes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both he and some of the people I spoke to -- let me describe the conditions in the camp first, and then we can make more sense of it. Open latrines, that is to say, holes full of excreta, so there was a terrible stink; inside the school, and it was surreal because they would have thing likes "photo club" written on the door, but inside would just be, I mean, what seemed to be sort of piles of people -- I cannot put it better than that -- the place was full to bursting, although the temperature was high; and the odd bit of bread perhaps being, sort of, you know, cut up to small pieces and distributed between a family. I sat down and talked to some people, mainly the women with their children, and one of them said: "Well, I came here voluntarily", and I thought, you know, "From what do you come here voluntarily?" She said that the violence in the villages was so much worse, that this was a safe place to come, at least here there was some sort of company, she said, I remember. They used the term "fighting" sometimes, sometimes they used the term "soldiers"; people talked about their houses being burnt, they did not have anywhere to go so they would come here. They also, some of them, said that they had paid to come into this place. The authority, the people -- I mean, later just before we left, taking this up with the people, the crowd you have seen on the video, they sort of made a virtue of the fact that people had come here voluntarily. They seemed to think that was some kind of mitigating aspect to all this. I drew just the opposite conclusion. I just thought, well, if you flee here, then what are you fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you get a chance to tour the medical facilities in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a sort of makeshift or what might be called hospital. There was a sort of sweaty, crowded room with a very paultry selection of bottles and a doctor whom we met and who was, rather like the people in the canteen of Omarska, seemed to be unwilling to go into too many details about what his work was. But he did give my colleague, Penny Marshal, who is the female reporter you have seen on the video, a roll of film which she took and which we later developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run the video, please, with the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is this the man that you see in the picture now representative of a number of the prisoners that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I may or may not have seen this particular man. I do not remember. But, yes, there were plenty of people like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could stop the tape there, please? You indicated earlier that you had interviewed people within the camp who related to you stories about Omarska and Keraterm in their experiences there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we learned more about Omarska and Keraterm from talking to the people in this camp than we had done in Omarska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could run this interview, please, with the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Continue the tape, please. Stop the tape there, please. Was that interview, brief interview, that we have heard representative of the interviews which you conducted with your colleagues in the camp, the information provided in that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that interview with the doctor, I mean, I was sort of mooching about at the back there. I mean, he was not going to -- he obviously was not saying very much. But one could gather, as we had done in the canteen, that what was not being said was as important as the few remarks he was able to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that the doctor gave you a film or actually gave a film to Penny Marshal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he gave it to her. She was doing the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did that film show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once developed, we saw that they were snapshots of the bodies -- I cannot say "bodies" -- the torsos and parts of the bodies of some of the people he had treated which showed severe bruising, widespread bruising, signs of beating and torture of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you left the Trnopolje camp where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went straight back to Belgrade -- a long drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you remain in the Belgrade area while your stories were published and broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was late in the evening of August 5th that we got back and I wrote my article about all this on the day of August 6th, and it was published on August 7th. The ITN material was transmitted on the night of the 6th. I would just like to say one thing before we leave Trnopolje which I think is important, if I may? Could I? I am sorry to -- I do not wish to ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that there was a man there from the Yugoslav Red Cross whom I interviewed, and it was particularly illuminating. I do not recall his name at the moment. I think it is Isic, but I can get it for you, if you want. I asked, I said: "What do you think of the conditions here?" He said: "I think they are fine". I asked him: "Have you been into Omarska?" and he said: "Yes, I have certainly been into Omarska, and I would say, in my professional assessment, that the health of the people there is very good except for some diarrhoea". Sorry, I wanted that on the record because that was an interview I did that I thought was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the reaction from the Bosnian Serb leadership to the reports you published in the TV coverage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A pretty explosive reaction all around. The Bosnian Serb leadership said various things. General Mladic, as I recall, said that the pictures that had been transmitted were forgeries and photo montages, or else pictures showing Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps. I cannot remember Dr. Karadzic's exact words, but they suggested that there had been some exaggeration -- I think they suggested that he was surprised by what had been discovered, while it was, forgive me, it was the Yugoslav President, Milan Panic, who said that anybody running such places would be punished and that they should be closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the reaction from the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outrage and resolved to do something about it. I recall President Bush saying that something to the effect of (and again I can get the exact quote, if you want it) that everything necessary must be done to end this, and to stop this, what is going on, and my hotel telephone on August 7th was ringing continually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might be a convenient time to take the afternoon recess.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. That last comment that you added, Mr. Vulliamy, as I recall earlier in the testimony, maybe several days ago, a witness told us that one of the camps was run somehow in conjunction with the Yugoslav International Red Cross or, at least, there was some involvement, unless I have mischaracterised the testimony. I had a question then as to how that could be involved. You have answered it now. So thank you for adding that or, at least, adding what they said about it. Thank you. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have brought an out of turn witness down to The Hague to follow on after this witness, but I have spoken to Mr. Keegan and he expects to take the rest of the day or almost the rest of the day, within a matter of minutes before 5.30. The witness is waiting in the witness room at the moment, but he has suffered a family bereavement some 40 days ago. According to his religion, he needs to attend a ceremony 40 days after the event. He is most anxious to leave if he possibly could. He is prepared to stay, of course, if necessary. But, as I think we will probably only get five minutes into his evidence, I am wondering if your Honours would mind giving him leave to go and come back at a later date to give his evidence, if that were possible? I do not think the court will be inconvenienced for any longer than about five minutes, if at all and probably not at all, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, how long do you think you will require for direct of Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would expect probably at a minimum 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will there be cross-examination of Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we anticipate there will be, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you think that you will require more than fifteen minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is difficult to say, but I do not think the court will be inconvenienced as we are aware of some other business that we have to deal with anyway, as a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is why I said 15 minutes. If you take 30 minutes and you take 15 minutes, then that would leave us 15 minutes to deal with the matters that we wanted to discuss. That witness may be excused for today, Mr. Niemann. Thank you for having him or her here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Him, I guess. We will resume with him on Tuesday at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He is out of turn, so we will go back to the correct order, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, thank you. Mr. Keegan, would you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): In addition to the responses from government officials, did the ICRC and other non-governmental organisations indicate that they were going to take action with regard to these camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, yes, they did. The reactions were varied across the board. I remember that the issue of camps on all sides being raised, and I remember almost universally the clamour being for Omarska at least to be closed down and I understand that it was almost immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have another meeting with Dr. Koljevic in Belgrade after the release of your stories about the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was a surprising one. This is Professor Nikola Koljevic, the Vice President of the Bosnian Serbs, Dr. Karadzic's Deputy, who had I think, although I cannot really tell, been in overall supervision of our visit. The atmosphere in Belgrade on the day of publication was not altogether hospitable. I spent most of the day in and out of television studios and talking to radio stations; and there was a surprising invitation from Professor Koljevic to tea and cakes at a hotel in Belgrade. I do not remember much about the conversation, but I do remember very vividly one remark from him that surprised me and it went something like this. He said in a semi-humorous, semi-mocking way: "So you found them then? Congratulations", he said, "you will do well out of this, young man. Took you a long time, did it not? Three months and all that happening so near Venice. All you people", by whom I think he meant the outside world, "all you people could worry about was poor, poor Sarajevo, multi-cultural cross-roads of Europe, university town", and he talked about the pretty girls in Sarajevo, poor Sarajevo, and concluded his remarks by saying: "None of you ever had your holidays in Prijedor, did you? No Winter Olympics in Omarska". It was an extraordinary monologue. He had given a press conference as well that day that I had attended, and I took his remark to be a piece of barbed wit and mockery at us as representing in a way the world for having gone on covering the war, as most of us had done, concentrating on the siege of, as he put it, "poor, poor multi-cultural Sarajevo", while they got on with the business, as he put it, "so near Venice" operating the camps that we had just uncovered with impugnity undetected and unhindered. It was a particularly bizarre conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the release of the articles about the camps, Omarska and Trnopolje, was there, in fact, a return by the ITN crew and others to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could we run the tape again, please, with the audio? Can we stop the tape there, please? Did you get an opportunity to look at that photograph which you have just pointed to in the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I looked at all the photographs. They are from the film that he had given Penny during the visit that I was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that particular photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A picture of a man's body bruised all down the side, if I identify it correctly, side and the back -- large scale bruising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That photograph came from the film which the doctor had given Penny Marshal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we can run the rest of the tape, please? Mr. Vulliamy, have you recently gone back to the Prijedor area and interviewed several of the persons whom you dealt with in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Among those people whom did you interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this is in February of this year, for reasons, part professional, part personal, I suppose, I wanted to see the place again now that it was possible to go back into that area, and the first thing we did, I did, was to go back to the camp itself, and the first people I spoke to were sentries at the gate of the front entrance this time to what was now an empty iron ore mining complex, disused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask those guards about the mining facility and about when it had been a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a circumspect way. I was not certain whether I was grata or not in the area and did not have papers from Pale to be there, so I was being circumspect at first, and asked them about -- first of all, we said: "Well, I hear that there were Serbian refugees here only last year", and they said, yes, there were, and talked about that a bit. Then: "So what about the camp? What about the concentration camp that was here a few years ago?" They said: "There was no camp here. That was all lies", and they were friendly enough. They said: "No, it was a mine, it was an iron ore mine. I should know, I was working here in the summer of 1992", and I thought, well, I believe that you were working here in 1992, but I do not believe that it was an iron ore mine because I can remember it. Of course, I did not let on that I had been there and, sort of, bit my tongue. I said: "Well, what about the television pictures then?" They said: "That was a video montage, Muslim propaganda. I know how they do it", and they were laughing, and we were laughing along with them, about how they would construct this video montage. I remember we asked: "Well, we have just driven from Prijedor and all the houses have been burned along the route, whose houses were they?" They said: "Oh, it is Muslims". We said: "Well, why did they go?" and these boys, the two of them, said: "I do not know. They just up and left". I do not know. It is as though I myself had packed my bags and gone. We returned to this matter of the camp: "Are you sure that in August there was no camp here?" and they said: "No, there was no camp, nothing, all lies". It was a pretty peculiar conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask them for their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- that conversation ended very surreally and it went like this: we had been taking notes and said: "What are your names, please?" They said: "No names. That is a secret. We have had a nice conversation, no names". I said: "Why not?" They said: "Oh, you know what can happen", and I am quoting as accurately as my memory serves -- I can give you the exact words if you want but this is pretty exactly what they said -- "You know how it is; you can be walking down the street one day and they will get you and take you to The Hague". "The Hague?" "Yes", they said. One of them said: "The Muslims know me, I know them, they know what I have done and that is how it is. They can just take you to The Hague. Look what happened to Dule Tadic". And I said: "Sorry, who?" "Dule Tadic in The Hague", and I said, well, my colleague actually said: "Do you know him?" and they said, this one man answered: "Oh, yes, we know him. He had a nice restaurant in Kozarac", and we let the conversation end with them saying: "He was getting some hassle from Muslims who were jealous of his restaurant and wanted to open a rival restaurant". Then I figured that it was best for the conversation to conclude and we left on amicable terms, if you like, but it was a curious twist to the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently interview some of the officials in Prijedor whom you had met in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought it would be interesting to seek out once again Mr. Drljaca, the police chief, Dr. Kovacevic, the man who when the television crews had returned to Trnopolje and Omarska during that last piece of video we had seen -- I was not there for that actually; I had gone off to do something else -- it was Kovacevic, the hefty man with the moustache and the t-shirt, you will recall, who was given the unenviable job of justifying the whole thing to the cameras which were by then, in terms of hundreds of them, down there quite a circus, not just the ITN that time; and he was given the task of justifying it. So I thought it would be interesting to go and find him again. I also wanted to find Mr. Stakic, the Mayor, the rather bald headed gentleman, who was nominally in charge of the operation, so I set about looking for all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, interview Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. He was permanently out of town which is either true or, in my experience, is the shorthand for "he does not want to talk to you".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you get to interview Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at length and this was a pretty extraordinary interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is your most vivid impression from that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it turned out that Dr. Kovacevic, it turned out that he was a doctor, he had told us back in 1992, if you recall, that he had been born in Jasenovac, in the concentration camp, and that was one reason why I wanted to go and talk to him. I found out that he was the director of the Prijedor hospital by this time. We went to see him at about half past nine to 10 o'clock in the morning. He told us that it had been a bad year -- a good year for grapes, but there was no -- the jam factories were all shut, shame to let them go to waste, as so he pulled a bottle of brandy out of the cupboard and started drinking it. During the two hours or so that we talked, he said that -- he drunk quite a lot of this brandy, and said things that I really was not expecting to hear. He said that Omarska had been planned as a detention centre, but had (and I quote almost exactly) "turned into something else". He said that he attributed that to what he called "collective madness". We asked him about the burned down houses along the road and the camps and he said: "It all looks very carefully planned if your view is from New York, but here on the ground when", and I think he said something, "when everything is coming apart inside your head, when things are breaking apart inside people's heads where everything is burning", and he talked about this collective madness. As the conversation continued and, to be frank, as he continued to drink the brandy, he seemed to become more and more haunted and his eyes were bulging. He was clearly tortured by what he was talking about. At one point I remember we asked him -- I was with a colleague from another newspaper -- we asked him: "How much responsibility do you take for this?" and he said -- I do have a transcript of this and we can check it against, if you like, but to my best recollection he said: "To say that I was -- if someone -- if I was" -- pardon me -- "if I was acquitted of a responsibility in that collective madness, that would not be right". He then qualified it by saying, and forgive me if I quote him in this way, the court, but this is what he said, he said: "If Dusko Tadic killed somebody and I did not, then it is not the same thing; but if I run this hospital well, then I am responsible for that success. If I run this hospital badly, then I am to blame". Those were his words, if not exactly, very closely. He then said that he wanted to get out, that he was like an animal trapped in the area. He said he wanted to go and practise abroad. He told us a bit about his career. He corrected his earlier remarks and said that he had not been born in Jasenovac, he had spent part of his childhood there, and gave quite a convincing account of how his aunt had taken him while his mother was fleeing through the woods around Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you during this conversation whether the situation that developed through 1990 into 1992 resulting in the conflict, did he categorise that as a destruction of Bosnia and why or why that was not necessary for that to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, despite his apparent remorse and acceptance of responsibility, he said that he thought it was, and I quote almost exactly "necessary to destroy Bosnia". He had kept the view that we cannot live together, that the Muslims and the Serbs cannot live together, and that it was necessary to destroy the country of Bosnia in which both lived at the same time. But he continued in a different vein when we asked him why he had left political life, and his answer was: "I left political life because I saw too many evil things. If you have to do things by killing people, well, then that is my personal secret", and he added shortly afterwards, "Now my hair is white, I do not sleep too well".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him about the link between what happened in Jasenovac and what happened in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, we talked a lot about Jasenovac. Perhaps I should say a little bit about what he told us about what he had done after Jasenovac. He said that he grown up after the war. He had gone to, of all places, Germany and studied anaesthetics and then come back to his home area. We said to him: "But, hang on, Jasenovac was the Croats. Omarska for which you were responsible was mostly Muslims, you know, why, what is the connection?" He came up with an intelligent reply. He said: "If you get bitten by a snake, you become afraid of lizards, but a snake is still a snake and a lizard is still a lizard".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you pointedly ask him what that reference was to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was clear in the conversation that the snake was the Croats and the lizards were the Muslims; that what he was saying was: "We were bitten by the Croats in my generation and we were afraid of the lizards", which I took to be the Muslims, "but the snake was still a snake and the lizard was still a lizard". For a man in his cups, he made sense in that way. We asked him, had he ever met any of the prisoners subsequently after the camp had closed down. He described an extraordinary episode. He said he had been called up for medical reasons to a frontline near Doboj where there was fighting, and that -- these frontlines are often only metres apart and there was quite of lot of parle between the two sides during the dulls. Anyway, he said: "And there was a man on the other side of the trenches, on the other side, and I recognised him", he said, "he had been a prisoner". He described a conversation in which they played each other their various propaganda radios. He said: "He was playing me some Muslim music and Muslim stuff, and I was playing him our Serbian radio". He said we, together, we cursed those people. He said to me, and it was -- he said: "Oh, God, help me. He had been in Omarska". That was towards the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you also interview Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a different interview. I found him. By the way, I should say that before this year I did not know these people were "Dr." anything; you know, it was Stakic and Kovacevic. I did not know they were doctors. It turned out that Stakic, the President of this Crisis Staff, the Mayor of Prijedor, was also a doctor and he was now running a day care health centre. He came down to meet us at the health centre, and this was a very different interview. He was composed, well in control of himself. There was a glass of brandy, but only one and did not produce any remorse. It was a peculiar conversation. He had with him a man he introduced as his deputy at the health centre. We started talking about the war. He said exactly the same thing as he had told us those three years ago. Neither of these men, by the way, recognised me. He said, in fact, yes, he said there were 3,500 armed men in Kozarac. It was an exact repetition three years later of what he had said on that morning before we went into the camps. We asked about Omarska and the man introduced to us as his deputy suddenly butted in and said: "Omarska was a mine; there was no camp in Omarska". Dr. Stakic changed the theme slightly and said: "Oh, this is my lawyer", so now this man had become a lawyer. Mr. Stakic then directly contradicted what his lawyer had just said and said: "Oh, Omarska was a place where people were taken who had taken up arms against us, and they were being vetted as to whether or not they had started the insurrection against us. These were prisoners of war". So there is another version as to who was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did he describe the pictures that were shown on TV in 1992 after your visit to the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not actually recall. I think that the man introduced as the lawyer butted in at one point and said: "Oh, they were forgeries", and I think Mr. Stakic mumbled something about them being Serbian prisoners in Muslim camps. It was clear that this whole conversation was being taped. He started messing around with a tape recorder, and then it became clear that the man who had started off as the deputy, who then became the lawyer, was some sort of policeman or bodyguard, and our interpreter had recognised him and was trying to convey this to us with sign language, pointing to the tape recorder. The conversation ended, but we kept asking about Omarska, and the reply was always "Jasenovac", "Jasenovac", "Jasenovac", so we were going round and round. We would ask about one lot of camps and the reply would be about another lot of camps in the previous generation which I found interesting. We ended up, Dr. Stakic said -- it was dark outside by now -- he said: "It is very brave of you to be here with us at this time of night", which we took as a good cue to make our way back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him about the effect of the Serb fight and what the goal was for these years that the conflict had been going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that the Serbs were defending themselves, defending their people, and there was a line from his sort of this side kick man, the secret policeman, lawyer, whatever he was, who said that, you know: "We learned our history in concentration camps". Then we asked why he had left political office. He said that he had gone back to continue his specialisation in neuropsychiatry, but now he was going to stand again for the Mayor of Prijedor for Dr. Karadzic's SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see Major Milutinovic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, in Banja Luka, this was the military man, if you recall, and he had said: "Omarska, well, first let me say that the army had nothing to do with Omarska, it was run by the civilian authorities" which, to give him his credit is true. He then said: "If there had been anything going on that was awry in Omarska, then the army would have known about it, and I can tell you that the army did not know about it". This is the man who was in the camp with us with the sort of pointed hat on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was his position at the time you interviewed him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, well, he had been Colonel in 1992 -- sorry, he had been a Major in 1992, he was now a Colonel, and he was the personal spokesman for General Mladic and I think his Adjutant as well, a sort of spokesman and aide de camp. He said that, "How can there have been anything wrong in Omarska in August 1992? The journalists went to Omarska in 1992 and they found nothing". I bit my tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Finally, did you have an opportunity to speak again with Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we found him at his office in Banja Luka; quite spritely, speaks very good English. He is an authority on Shakespeare and likes to quote a lot of literary references. Two long conversations. He was the only man to whom I gave my name and identified myself. I reminded him that he had mocked me, as it were, me being the outside world, for taking so long in uncovering the camps. He apologised for mocking us, and said that Omarska was one of those things that was very difficult to control, and talked about his politics, his views, and what the war had meant to him and talked about -- I used the term yesterday "racial memory" -- he talked a lot about racial memory, how the Serbs were proud of their racial memory, and how he regarded this as the third great revolt of the Serbs; the other two having been against the Ottomans and the Austro-Hungarians. He talked mainly in this rather puffed up way. There was a very strange moment when he went over to the window and stared out of the window at the square below, and appeared to lose himself in his thoughts and started talking about disinternment of bones. It was not quite clear what bones he was talking about. He said it was 1989 when the Serbs were digging up their dead from the war and moving them elsewhere in the country. He started talking about children's shoes interred and things. It was very strange and then came to his senses and came back and talked about the war. He accepted -- he was obsessed by lies and deceit and talked about propaganda a lot, and seemed to regard everything that we, the mass media, had done during the war as some sort of grand conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he particularly categorise certain aspects of reports that had been published about certain aspects of the conflict ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- in reference to this discussion on propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. In fact, I mean, he is an expert on theatre and Shakespeare. His books are quite well know. They are obligatory if you are a student of English in former Yugoslavia. He portrayed the whole thing as though it was some kind of grand drama, hyped up by the west. He said: "You began with the demonic Serb, then you moved into the massacre of children, poor little children, in Sarajevo -- very effective". He was sort of congratulating us, rather like he was back in 1992. "Then you started talking about concentration camps with all the resonance that has with the Nazis. Then you moved into rape and the violation of women", and made some rather uncouth jokes about that. "Then, finally, you end up with this grand word 'genocide'", and he treated it all as though it was a, sort of, great drama, a piece of theatre, that we, the mass media, had constructed to depict his people's defence of themselves as he saw it. It was most illuminating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the particular comment he made with regards to the allegations of rape as a war crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but it was something to the effect of that Napoleon had said that rape could not be a crime in war, and it was something about how a woman with her skirt up can run faster than a man with his trousers done, if I recall. He thought that was quite funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he make reference to the pictures which were published, in fact, in The Guardian of Fikret Alic behind the wire in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I felt secure to do so, I challenged him on it. I said: "What about what we have found? What about the torsos behind the wire?" And he said: "Oh, there was one man with tuberculosis", he said, "there was a man with tuberculosis, and the media found him and they took pictures of him and blew it all over the world. That man was suffering from TB".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he, like Dr. Kovacevic, make reference to the destruction of Yugoslavia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said it was necessary and talked about the future Republika Srpska as a place that would be a country for the Serbs and so on. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he place the responsibility for the destruction on the JNA within this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one interesting line, yes. He said towards the beginning of the conversation: "It was necessary for the JNA to destroy Yugoslavia".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did he categorise the conflict that was going on with regard to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, you know, he set it in the history of the struggle of the Serbian people and their quest to survive against these endlessly constructive enemies out to decimate them, the third great Serb rebellion and in this melodramatic, sort, historical context -- sorry, I would just like to add about the boy having TB; he was referring to Fikret Alic, I think. I subsequently met Fikret Alic, fattened out quite a bit. He did not have TB. I would just like to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the event there is no cross-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have only one question. Early in your evidence, and by now you may have forgotten it, you contrasted the Serb view of the Croats with the Serb view of the Muslims. I think you described the description of the Muslims as being filthy gypsies, that was the term used, they were dirty, they bred like rabbits. I had gained the impression that the Muslims tended to be in Bosnia Herzegovina the wealthier class, the urban dwellers, the by and large professional people, and so on. Am I right in that and, if so, how does that reconcile with the contempt shown for them, as you put it, by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In most parts of the country that is absolutely accurate, a social point. This is a broad brush. In Eastern Bosnia there is a fairly sizeable Muslim peasantry and a greater or smaller Muslim peasantry elsewhere in the country. There is also a Muslim industrial working strata in central Bosnia. But the history of the people is that they were, as it were, the governors of under the Ottoman tutelage and were large landowners. During the 30s they were largely stripped of their land owning and urbanised and became the intelligentsia. So, yes, particularly in the area we are talking about, the Prijedor region, one would find from what I can gather in most villages the chances are that the headmaster and the small businessman would be a Muslim. However, I stand by obviously the characterization which I heard over and over again, filthy gypsies, and so on. It is a difficult one to reconcile. I do not want to try to get into political psychoanalysis, but perhaps, and there are historical precedents for this I am sure, in the resentment of the relative economic superiority or relative economic comfort of this group of people, there might have been some sort of attempt to degrade them beneath those who harboured that resentment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think I will not take you any further. You at least confirm my general impression of their status.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, from what I know. There are people better qualified than I to talk about the sociology in makeup of that country, but from the sort of people that one met and from everything one heard, yes, in the main by the time that community had urbanised, certainly in Sarajevo itself, the Muslims tended to be the shopkeepers, the businessmen, the intelligentsia and the middle class in quite a lot of these communities, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have one question. Earlier, just maybe 10 minutes ago, you said regarding the Omarska camp, during an interview you said that to give him his credit it was true that Omarska was run by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Major Milutinovic, as he was in 1992, Colonel Milutinovic as he was in 1995, was I think trying to make the point, "If we are going to talk about Omarska, I am a military man. Omarska was not run by the military; it was run by the civilian authorities in Prijedor." When I meant by to give him his credit, what I meant was it was a fair point inasmuch as it was clear to us during our meeting in Prijedor at the Civic Centre and during our conversation with Colonel Arsic and the civilian authorities, that it was the civilian authorities and the police that were running Omarska, not the army. So that Colonel Milutinovic's detachment from Omarska was in a way valid in so far as, although he had been with us in the camp, and I am sure knew perfectly well what was going on in the camp, he did not have formal direct authority over it. The formal direct, formal direct authority over Omarska for the running of the camp was in the hands of the Mayor of Prijedor, Mr. Stakic's deputy, Mr. Koracevic and the Chief of Police, Mr. Drljaca, as far as we could ascertain and as far as we were told. So I suppose he was trying to say: "We will talk about Omarska, but I was not in control of it; it was not under military authority."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keegan, are there additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Is there any objection to Mr. Vulliamy being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are excused, sir. Thank you very much for coming. (The witness withdrew). We need to go into closed session at this time to talk about the motion, one motion at least that the Prosecutor has filed. (Hearing in Closed Session).

procedural_notes.text: (The court adjourned for a short time)
